item.title: Metal-Free Spin Crossover Through Nitrogen-Intercalated Graphene Under Pressure
item.description: Spin crossover (SCO) phenomena, in which the spin state of an atom changes due to an external stimulus, have been the subject of ongoing research interest to this day. However, the considered atoms have been limited to transition metals like iron or cobalt. In this theoretical study, we show for the first time that external pressure can cause a nitrogen atom, i.e., a non-metal, to transit from a high spin (HS) to a low spin (LS) configuration. This nitrogen atom is located between two graphene sheets (N@Graphene) to mediate anisotropic pressure, serving as a proof-of-principle system on a periodic density functional theory (DFT) level. With increasing pressure, the distance between nitrogen and the graphene sheets decreases, leading to a SCO at a pressure below 5 GPa. To understand more about the mechanism behind the SCO, a finite model system, N@Circumcoronene, was constructed to allow the application of various electronic structure analysis tools for finite systems. These tools confirm that the SCO is the result of a closed-shell-dominated interaction in the sandwich structure. This work introduces a promising basis for the realization of a new class of materials with pressure-sensitive SCO involving main group atoms.

item.title: AutoSPS-D2B: Automated Solid-Phase Synthesis Expands the Reaction Scope for Direct-to-Biology Libraries
item.description: Direct-to-biology (D2B) has emerged as a powerful accelerant in early drug discovery, bypassing compound purification to compress the design-make-test-analyse (DMTA) cycle. However, the chemistry underpinning D2B libraries is limited to just a few sequential transformations using assay-compatible reagents and solvents. By contrast, solid-phase synthesis (SPS) empowers a far broader range of reactions and is highly amenable to multistep synthesis, yet its potential as a source for D2B libraries remains largely underexplored. In this study, we develop AutoSPS-D2B, a fully automated solid-phase synthesis workflow that converts multistep, resin-bound chemistry into crude screening libraries that can be assayed directly, expanding reaction scope well beyond the reach of solution-phase D2B. We applied AutoSPS-D2B to explore several distinct chemotypes as allosteric ligands for the immuno-oncology target CCR2. Good agreement was observed in the relative binding affinity trends between crude and pure screening compounds, enabling streamlined ranking of analogues and prioritisation of hits for further investigation. When applied to the advancement of a previously underexplored CCR2 hit, AutoSPS-D2B enabled an analogue space of more than 1,700 building block combinations to be rapidly sampled, leading to optimised compounds with up to six-fold binding affinity improvements in just two DMTA cycles. This work establishes automated SPS as a versatile and efficient engine for D2B-driven hit-to-lead discovery.

item.title: CIPER: Interpretable Permeability Predictions Guide Cyclic Peptide Editing
item.description: Each new analogue in a synthetic cyclic-peptide library requires synthesis and permeability measurement, making the choice of an edit consequential. Molecular difference learning predicts the effect of a modification; we ask whether explicit structural comparisons can also identify the measured analogues supporting its selection or parent retention. CIPER, short for Context-Integrated Potential Edit Regression, learns assay-matched permeability differences through a product of atomic and cyclic-residue kernels. Each prediction is an exact sum of signed training-molecule contributions. A comparison of 18 fixed-ranking and sampling methods covers 286 parent pools containing 4,213 measured candidate pairs. CIPER gives the highest one-query mean gain among the 13 methods sharing the permitted training labels under equal chemical-component weights. One CIPER query recovers 0.518 log10 units of improvement, exceeding 0.491 from four random queries; four queries reduce random-selection regret by 75.1%. Separate tests on 1,213 complete panels distinguish choosing an improving product from identifying parents worth retaining. Signed contributions expose supporting and opposing analogues in successful and missed recommendations, motivating synthesis tests across controlled changes in ring, tail and stereochemical context. CIPER makes the chemical evidence behind early candidate enrichment directly inspectable.

item.title: A mechanistic insight into the role of triplet states in excited-state deactivation of dibenzothiophene: a new fate for green chemistry
item.description: The environmental impact of petroleum derivatives is a current threat which needs to be studied and tackled in the present and near future. In this context, obtaining new insight about the degradation and remediation possibilities of polyaromatic sulphur heterocycles, and particularly dibenzothiophene, is a challenge requiring the full attention of the academic community. Thus, we have studied the dibenzothiophene excited state decay from a theoretical perspective, resorting to multiconfigurational methods, in order to obtain a full photophysical picture which until now was incomplete. Our results reveal the transitory generation of triplet species which supports the possible reactivity and desulphurization processes which were recently reported for this system.

item.title: synthmc: a precedent-based synthesizability score for transition metal complexes
item.description: Data-driven methods are increasingly being used for the in silico discovery of transition metal complexes (TMCs), ranging from machine learning models for high-throughput screening and generative models proposing new candidates to evolutionary algorithms for their de novo design. However, computationally discovered or designed TMCs are only rarely realized experimentally, in part because their synthesis is difficult and often not considered during the design process. At the same time, established synthetic accessibility scores for organic small molecules cannot be transferred to TMCs beyond their constituent ligands, as their fragment-based heuristics and molecular representations do not capture the influence of the metal center, coordination mode, and steric effects on coordinability. Here, we present synthmc, a precedent-based synthesizability score for TMCs that combines the precedent of ligands, coordination environments, and degrees of steric crowding in a reference corpus constructed from experimentally reported complexes in the Cambridge Structural Database. Evaluated on random and time-based validation sets, synthmc assigns, on average, lower scores to more recently reported complexes, consistent with their reduced precedent, indicating its ability to identify novel chemistry. We hope that synthmc will help to prioritize synthetically accessible candidates in high-throughput screening and generative design of TMCs and, more broadly, motivate the development of more comprehensive synthesizability assessments for TMCs, for example based on retrosynthetic approaches or expert evaluations.

item.title: The Same Edit, a Different Outcome: Relational Learning for Cyclic Peptide Permeability
item.description: The same local modification can enhance cyclic-peptide permeability in one chemical background and reduce it in another. Molecular difference learning predicts such changes from structure pairs, yet whole-molecule descriptors can merge stereochemically distinct edits. We test whether the residue relationships changed by an edit supply additional predictive information. Our edit-relational Gaussian process combines parent descriptors and their changes with signed counts of gained and lost residue relationships, preserving stereochemistry and ring, branch and tail connectivity. Across 286 parent pools and 4,213 measured pairs, the best measured improvement over the parent after two queries is 0.588 versus 0.54 log10 permeability units under equal component weights. Relational inputs improve this gain in all five evaluated chemical components under matched fitting and initial-mean ranking. Measured interaction panels contain 13 edit-preference reversals among 72 distinct-site comparisons, exposing the background dependence that the representation is designed to capture. Exact finite-pool analysis separates candidate resolution from measurement allocation. Controls sharing the first mean-ranked query locate the principal measured benefit in the representation and initial ranking. The findings motivate matched-edit experiments on new parents to test whether these relationships predict how permeability benefits transfer between backgrounds. An edited residue’s changing relationships provide a concrete, predictively useful description of its chemical context.

item.title: Contact-electro-catalytic degradation of 4-hydroxybenzoic acid using PTFE
item.description: This study introduces an ultrasound-powered contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) method for degrading 4-hydroxybenzoic acid (HBA) using polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) microparticles. Under neutral conditions, the system achieved over 99% HBA degradation in aqueous solutions. Mechanistic analysis confirms that hydroxyl radicals act as the primary oxidants. HBA degradation proceeds via primary hydroxylation and secondary decarboxylation pathway. The effects of acidic and alkaline conditions were investigated, demonstrating the non-innocent role of counter ions. Furthermore, recycling tests showed that the PTFE catalyst retains high structural integrity and consistent degradation efficiencies (96%–99%) of HBA across consecutive cycles. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultrasound-driven CEC as a robust technology for wastewater remediation.

item.title: Improved Reproducibility of FT-ICR Mass Spectra for Organic Matter by Minimizing Electronic Noise Peaks and Low-abundance Peaks with Few Occurrences
item.description: Peak reproducibility is a major factor that affects the reliability of Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) spectra of dissolved organic matter (DOM), which was addressed by a newly proposed workflow, namely parallel samples representation by similar samples (PSRSS). The performance of the workflow was validated by parallel measurements and experimental replicates. Inspection of isotopic and homologous peaks in the PSRSS workflow enabled elimination of electronic noise peaks and low-abundance peaks with few occurrences, significantly decreased the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, and improved the molecular formula assignment ratio with only minor effects on the assigned formulae. The Bray-Curtis dissimilarity threshold (55% to 60% or quartile) was proposed to cluster FT-ICR MS spectra for DOM samples with similar molecular composition. The noise peak removal performance was further improved for the similar molecular composition samples by excluding outlier spectra and less frequently occurring peaks via the PSRSS workflow. Moreover, the reliability of DOM molecular characterization was significantly improved by the PSRSS workflow. Overall, our findings demonstrated the feasibility of the PSRSS workflow to serve as a reliable, labor-saving method to remove electronic noise peaks and cluster spectra, yielding reliable spectral 3information for multiple independent FT-ICR MS spectra.

item.title: Comprehensive Two-dimensional liquid chromatography technology and its applications in the field of traditional Chinese medicine
item.description: Comprehensive two-dimensional liquid chromatography (LC×LC) represents a significant breakthrough in modern separation science. Theoretically, it leverages the synergistic effect of separation capabilities across both dimensions to substantially enhance peak capacity, providing robust technical support for analyzing complex systems such as traditional Chinese medicine. However, after nearly a decade of development and application, substantial gaps remain between its theoretical advantages and practical performance in TCM analysis. This paper systematically examines the current application status of LC×LC in TCM analysis and addresses key challenges, including strategic dilemmas in separation mode selection, engineering challenges related to system compatibility, and insufficient data processing automation. Furthermore, based on the characteristics of TCM chemical constituents, targeted technological development pathways are proposed to guide substantive advancements in this technique for modern TCM research.

item.title: EasyNMR: shareable flow-based workflows for reproducible analysis of NMR and other scientific data
item.description: Spectroscopic studies increasingly require analyses beyond what standard software offers, yet the programs that make them possible are often developed in single laboratories, are hard to maintain and are difficult to share. Here we present EasyNMR, a web-native platform that applies flow-based programming to the analysis of NMR spectra and other scientific data, turning each analysis into a shareable, executable workflow. The workflow is built from flow objects that exchange data predominantly in the Core Scientific Dataset Model, so every step receives self-describing data without lossy conversion. EasyNMR runs in the browser without installation, reads the common NMR data formats and connects to containerised back-end services that run established programs such as SIMPSON, MRSimulator, SLEEPY, ShiftML, and PIPNet, keeping legacy codes alive. The examples include lineshape fitting with parameter uncertainties, multi-field and multidimensional analyses, a ligand titration, relaxation analysis, spectrum and spin-system prediction from molecular structures, and customised workflows for non-specialists. The fitted parameters agree with literature values. Because a workflow is itself a shareable file, a complete analysis, including every figure in this paper, can be reopened, inspected and reused by others from a single link.

item.title: Understanding the Orchestrating Role of TLR2 in Differential Heterodimerization
Stepwise reduction of a porphyrin nanowire: minimal structural reorganization up to the open-shell tetraanion
item.description: π-Conjugated porphyrin oligomers serve as molecular wires: they exhibit high single-molecule conductance and excellent cycling kinetics as organic active electrode materials. These applications require systems in which charge/discharge cycles cause minimal changes in molecular geometry. Here, we use a butadiyne-linked porphyrin dimer as a model compound to show that its chemical reduction with alkali metals leads to subtle changes in the bond lengths in the resulting multiply charged anions, as revealed crystallographically. The small structural changes are consistent with a low inner-sphere reorganization energy, as expected for an efficient redox-active molecular wire. π-Bond Delocalization Function (π-BDF) analysis shows that successive reduction increases π-electron delocalization within the porphyrin cores, while the involvement of the butadiyne linker is strongly charge- and spin-state-dependent. The previously unknown, structurally characterized tetraanion has an open-shell singlet diradical ground state with a thermally accessible triplet state, separated by 14.2 kJ mol−1, as established experimentally by EPR spectroscopy and supported by DFT calculations. The two open-shell states retain nearly identical covalent-delocalization topologies and differ primarily in the organization and coupling of their two unpaired electrons. Prolonged reaction with lithium metal leads to demetallation of these zinc porphyrins and cleavage of the butadiyne, forming an acetylene-appended porphyrin monomer.

item.title: Interfacial Organization and Direction-Dependent Transport of Hydrocarbons in Graphene Slit Pores
item.description: Hydrocarbon transport in nanopores depends on the spatial organization of the confined fluid. We investigate this relationship through molecular dynamics simulations of methane, benzene, and n-octane between fixed graphene sheets, varying temperature and pore width. Density profiles and orientational distributions are combined with lateral mobility and wall-to-wall exchange to characterize structure and motion in interfacial and interior populations. Surface-aligned benzene layers sustain appreciable lateral mobility, whereas tightly confined n-octane exhibits strongly suppressed translation despite orientational rearrangement. Methane displays weak regional contrast in lateral mobility in the wider pores. In wide-pore benzene, molecular redistribution between interfacial and interior environments and orientational broadening accompany a nonmonotonic thermal response of lateral mobility. Lateral translation and wall-to-wall exchange exhibit distinct dependences on pore width, reflecting different constraints on motion within adsorbed layers and transfer between interfaces. These results connect adsorption and molecular packing to spatially heterogeneous transport and identify how molecular architecture and pore geometry shape motion along the interfaces and across the pore.

item.title: Photoswitchable Carbon Nanohoops with Light-Controlled Fullerene Recognition and Charge Transfer
item.description: Cycloparaphenylenes (CPPs) are among the most versatile carbon nanohoops for fullerene recognition. However, their structural, electronic, and host-guest properties are fixed by molecular composition. Here, we introduce a different concept by incorporation of a diarylethene (DAE) photoswitch into the CPP framework, thereby transforming a static carbon nanohoop into a light-responsive supramolecular host. DFT calculations reveal that photoisomerization of the incorporated DAE unit reversibly expands the nanohoop cavity by approximately 1 Å, enabling light-controlled switching of fullerene selectivity among C60, C70, and C84. Beyond structural changes, photoisomerization also reorganizes the electronic structure and excited-state properties of the host-guest complexes. Ring closure introduces a previously inaccessible DAE-centered charge-transfer (CT) state in addition to the conventional CPP-to-fullerene CT pathway. Although this new CT state is strongly stabilized in polar media, electron-transfer kinetics indicate that rapid charge recombination limits its population, whereas the conventional CT state remains long-lived. These findings suggest that incorporation of a DAE photoswitch enables reversible control over cavity size, guest selectivity, exciton localization, and electron-transfer dynamics, yielding adaptive, stimuli-responsive carbon nanohoops with broad potential in photoactive materials.

item.title: FrictionSim2D: A High-Throughput Molecular Simulation Framework to Screen the Friction of Two-Dimensional Materials
Donor priming and conformational control in arginine N-rhamnosylation by the glycosyltransferase EarP
item.description: EarP is an unusual glycosyltransferase that rhamnosylates R32 of bacterial elongation factor P (EF-P), catalyzing glycosylation of a poorly nucleophilic guanidinium moiety. How donor and acceptor are organized to enable this rare reaction remains incompletely understood. Here, we report the synthesis and use of complementary low-reactivity analogs of dTDP-rhamnose (dTDP-Rha) to capture structural states associated with substrate recognition and turnover by EarP from Neisseria meningitidis, supported by biochemical assays of glycosyl transfer. Seven crystal structures, including ternary complexes, reveal distinct rearrangements of the donor and acceptor that support a model of significant substrate reorganization preceding productive chemistry. These include a Michaelis-like configuration that positions the anomeric center for attack by R32EF-P and suggests a possible contribution of sugar-ring distortion to productive donor geometry, whereas product complexes containing α-2F-rhamnosylated EF-P demonstrate the transfer of the fluorinated sugar with inversion of anomeric configuration. Together, these structures support a model in which productive substrate organization involves coordinated positioning of the acceptor and significant reorientation of the sugar donor. This structural framework provides insights into how EarP controls this unusual N-glycosylation reaction and highlights donor conformational rearrangements as a potentially broader feature of glycosyltransferase catalysis.

item.title: Bayesian Optimization Outperforms Experts for Spectral Model Development
item.description: Indirect Hard Modeling (IHM) is a physically motivated approach for quantitative spectral analysis that can account for nonlinear spectral changes, provides loweffort calibration, and allows extrapolation. However, realizing the full potential of IHM requires careful adjustment of model parameters and spectral preprocessing settings, which is typically performed manually and relies on expert knowledge. To address this limitation, we investigate Bayesian Optimization (BO) as a strategy for efficient IHM parameter tuning with mixed continuous, discrete, and categorical parameter spaces. We couple six alternative BO frameworks differing in surrogate model and sampling strategy with Peaxact, a state-of-the-art commercial software for IHM. We compare the calibration performance and computation time. We develop four spectroscopic models based on literature datasets. The corresponding IHM models in the form of published parameter settings serve only as benchmarks and are not used to initialize the optimization. We thus demonstrate that IHM models can be automatically optimized without expert intervention nor prior selected configurations. The results show that BO outperforms the published models, ranging from marginal changes to reductions of approximately 50% in cumulative cross-validation RMSE and approximately 60% in cumulative prediction RMSE, 1 with mean runtimes of approximately five hours or less on a standard desktop computer, supporting practical applicability. Moreover, the configurations obtained via BO partially agree with the expert-selected settings, indicating that BO can identify reasonable calibration settings from scratch. Overall, the findings demonstrate that BO can improve IHM model accuracy, reduce manual calibration effort, and support the broader use of IHM in spectroscopy.

item.title: Gain, Retention, or Loss of Aromaticity upon Surface Adsorption: π-Electron Systems on Cu(111)
item.description: Understanding the interactions between metal surfaces and the π-electron systems of flat-lying polycyclic conjugated hydrocarbons is central to designing metal–organic interfaces and on-surface synthesis. This surface interaction is sometimes rationalized in terms of aromaticity, which is usually evaluated for gas phase model systems and rarely for adsorbed molecules. Here, we use density functional theory to study changes in geometric and electronic aromaticity for 22 π-electron systems upon adsorption on Cu(111), from physisorption to strong chemisorption. Surprisingly, the change in aromaticity does not simply follow the interaction strength. Instead, population of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital causes two competing effects: bond length equalization, driven by the gas phase bond length alternation, and bond elongation, determined by the adsorption height. Consequently, physisorbed molecules retain their aromaticity, while chemisorbed molecules can gain, locally alter, or lose it. The change in aromaticity can be decomposed into a deformation contribution (structural change upon adsorption) and an interaction contribution (direct electronic effect of the surface). Geometric indices capture only the deformation contribution, which shows the same trends in the electronic indices. The interaction contribution is negligible for the critical-point-based index but lowers the bond-order-based aromaticity of all molecules. This reflects the overlap of molecular and surface electron densities rather than a loss of aromaticity. Thus, geometric aromaticity indices, which require only the adsorption structure, provide enough insights into the changes upon adsorption. The gas phase aromaticity is therefore only a partial guide, as aromaticity at interfaces is a property of the full molecule–surface system.

item.title: Tautomerism and Diradical Character: Chemical and Electronic Structure of a High-Performance Organic Electrode Material
item.description: Bis-tetraaminobenzoquinone (TAQ) is a high-performance organic electrode material whose molecular structure remains a subject of debate, which we address in this joint experimentaltheoretical study. Using density functional theory (DFT) across multiple scales, from isolated molecules to periodic crystal structures, this work provides an atomistic insight into the structural and electronic complexity of TAQ. Our analysis reveals a rich tautomeric landscape, identifying two energetically competitive forms: the originally proposed piperazine tautomer and a proton-shifted variant featuring a pyrazine-based core and NH3 groups at the periphery. Crucially, both tautomers exhibit near-degenerate closed-shell singlet, open-shell singlet (diradical character), and triplet states. We attribute the open-shell electronic character to resonance forms that contain quinoid-like and aromatic diradical motifs. The importance of open-shell states is confirmed by variable-temperature electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, which detects a ∆mS = 2 transition and yields a singlet–triplet gap of only 0.4–0.7 meV. Constrained DFT configuration interaction (cDFT-CI) calculations demonstrate that this open-shell character can enhance efficient electron transfer. These findings resolve discrepancies in experimental NMR data, previously interpreted as evidence for the structurally related TAPT compound, by showing that they arise naturally from a tautomeric form of TAQ. This tautomer accounts for the elusive origin of the organic spin, which stems from its unique open-shell electronic structure.

item.title: Programmable Self-Sorting in Multi-Component Coordination Cage Systems via Ligand Tethering
item.description: Control over self-sorting in multi-component metal-organic self-assembly remains a major challenge as mixtures of ligands commonly yield statistical distributions of products. Integrative and heteromeric completive self-sorting regimes are both attractive non-statistical outcomes, but each typically requires system-specific design; switching between the two cannot readily be achieved within a single ligand set. Here, we show that a simple tethering strategy enables programmable self-sorting in heteroleptic Pd(II) coordination cages by chelation. Covalent linking of ligand scaffolds allowed systems to be selectively directed towards either heteromeric completive or (pseudo-)integrative selfsorting. Using this approach, we demonstrate the selective formation of i) a single heteroleptic Pd2LaLbLc2-type cage, and defined mixtures of ii) two or iii) three different heteroleptic assemblies without changing the backbone geometry or donor groups of the ligands. The ability to access distinct self-sorting regimes provides a simple and versatile strategy for high-fidelity assembly of complex multi-component coordination cage systems.

item.title: Cation Identity and Framework Topology Govern CO2 Adsorption in FAU, MER, and RHO Zeolites
item.description: Aluminosilicates are widely investigated for carbon capture and utilization. Understanding the mechanism of CO2 adsorption in these materials is crucial for designing efficient carbon-capture materials. However, atomistic-level investigation of CO2 interaction and dynamics within confined pores of zeolites remains challenging due to two main factors: the need for local characterization techniques capable of probing changes in the chemical environment of active sites at the atomic scale, and the predominantly non-covalent nature of CO2 and adsorbent interactions under confinement. Advanced magic-angle-spinning (MAS) solid-state NMR spectroscopy enables localized characterization of zeolites by probing different nuclei. In this study, all possible nuclei in Na- and Li-exchanged and other ion-exchanged FAU, MER, and RHO zeolites are investigated using advanced multinuclear solid-state NMR experiments, including multiple-quantum magic-angle spinning (MQMAS) and heteronuclear correlation spectroscopy (HETCOR). We are still working on some experiments, such as exchange spectroscopy (EXSY), rotational-echo saturation-pulse double-resonance (RESPDOR), and dipolar heteronuclear multiple-quantum coherence (D-HMQC), to elucidate the influence of CO2 on their respective environments. We performed all solid-state NMR measurements at two different magnetic fields. We then derived conclusions about how different cations and framework nuclei participate in CO2 adsorption. A key experimental challenge was performing all solid-state NMR measurements and CO2 adsorption using the same zeolite sample packed in a solid-state NMR rotor. This challenge was addressed through the engineering development of a custom-built gas adsorption setup for solid-state NMR rotors. In Na- and Li-FAU, CO2 uptake induced reorganization of the cation sites through migration to the supercage. In contrast, MER and RHO exhibited indications of breathing and trapdoor mechanisms, respectively, upon CO2 uptake.

item.title: Scalable Density-Based Bootstrap Embedding with Perturbative Triples for Large Molecular Systems
item.description: Extending density-based bootstrap embedding (BE) with perturbative triples to large molecules requires control of both fragment solver cost and tensor storage. We present a restricted and unrestricted BE-CCSD(T) implementation combining density-fitted embedding transformations, fragment parallelism, and streamed contractions of triples density contributions. Explicit one-and two-particle terms and the correction to the coupled-cluster multipliers are retained without assembling a molecular two-particle density matrix or storing a complete triples tensor. item.title: Microplastic Identification by Temperature-Resolved Fluorescence Imaging
item.description: Heating Nile Red-stained microplastics on a filter while imaging their fluorescence allows to determine their flowthrough temperatures, associated with melting or softening of the polymers. Using a widefield microscope and a consumer-grade camera we classify HDPE, LDPE, PP, PVC and PMMA by RGB values and flow-through temperature.

item.title: Non-Orthogonal Exciton Theory Including Charge Transfer Effects for Strongly Coupled Chromophores
Complete Top-down Sequencing of Therapeutic Phosphorodiamidate Morpholino Oligomers by Multimodal Ion Activation in Both Polarities
item.description: Phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers (PMOs) are an important class of approved antisense therapeutics whose neutral backbone presents significant challenges for tandem mass spectrometric sequencing. Here, we evaluate multiple ion activation strategies on a timsOmni™ prototype in both electrospray polarities using the approved PMO drugs viltolarsen (21-mer) and eteplirsen (30-mer). In negative ion mode, resonance collisioninduced dissociation (RCID) and infrared multiphoton dissociation (IRMPD) each provided complete sequence coverage for both PMOs from charge states generated under standard infusion conditions. Electron detachment dissociation followed by RCID (EDD-RCID, MS3) also achieved full coverage of viltolarsen and produced diagnostic d- and z-type ions that retained the labile dimethylamino group, which was lost during purely vibrational activation. In positive ion mode, conventional CID resulted primarily in nucleobase loss with no backbone cleavage. However, electron-based activation methods, including electron capture dissociation (ECD) and electron-induced dissociation (EID), combined with supplementary RCID of the radical cation, restored backbone fragmentation and enabled complete sequence coverage. Propylene carbonate (PC) proved valuable to achieve complete coverage by generating the higher charge states required for EDD-RCID and positive-mode electron-based workflows. Together, these results outline several effective activation strategies for PMO sequencing.

item.title: A fluorescence polarization probe for rapid and quantitative analysis of interactions between Rubisco and small molecules
Why Pairwise Force Fields Can Reproduce Ionic Conductivity but Not Solvation Shells
item.description: Pairwise force fields with scaled ionic charges are routinely validated against ionic conductivity or other collective transport measurements and used to interpret Li+ solvation and transport in battery electrolytes. We test this practice for 1.5 M LiFSI in dimethyl ketone with ab initio molecular dynamics, a fine-tuned machine learning potential, a newly developed polarizable force field, and a pairwise force field with charge scaling, compared with both Raman probes of the Li+ shell through computed bound-to-free cross-sections. The pairwise model reproduces the ionic conductivity, yet places 51% of anions in contact with Li+ (21% measured) and 4.8 ligands around the cation (4.0 from first principles). No adjustment of pair parameters removes the excess acetone, as ligand polarization is non-additive, costing a fifth ligand 22–25 kJ mol−1 of polarization energy, and favors acetone over the anion. The many-body models revise the experimental interpretation: Li+ moves vehicularly with a compact four-coordinate shell and ion pairing barely lowers the conductivity, which reflects the low viscosity of acetone rather than the fraction of solvent-separated ions. Agreement with transport therefore validates neither the solvation shell nor the transport mechanism, and we propose a validation protocol built on solvent-side spectroscopic observables.Pairwise v many-body paradigms for the study of battery electrolytes, and comparison with Raman spectra

item.title: Structure Before Sequence: Physicochemical Catalytic Organization and Biological Reconstruction
item.description: Biological catalysis depends on highly organized protein and RNA architectures whose reproducible construction is itself sequence-supported, creating a familiar circularity in discussions of catalytic origins. This Perspective separates two questions that are often treated together: what physical organization is sufficient for catalytic function, and what sequencesupported biology adds to make selected catalytic architectures reproducibly reconstructable. Experimental systems spanning inorganic nanoparticles, supramolecular assemblies, metal–organic frameworks, nucleic-acid-organized catalysts, and proteins reveal multiple routes by which catalytic possibilities can be constrained, integrated, and made increasingly programmable without a complete biological reconstruction system. A complementary principle is provided by the Inorganic Code, defined here as the accessible electronic and catalytic potential arising principally from electronically reconfigurable transition-metal d states and their ligand-mediated d–p interactions. Nanozyme and metalloprotein chemistry show that these metal-centered possibilities persist across materially different architectures, while ligand identity, coordination, hydration, structural organization, and environment determine their expression. Fe–S chemistry provides a representative case in which physicochemical continuity does not require structural 2 inheritance: related redox and electron-transfer possibilities occur in minerals, assembled clusters, peptide-associated systems, and proteins under different organizational constraints. We therefore propose Structure Before Sequence as a statement of physicochemical priority rather than compulsory historical succession. Catalytic function requires an operating physical architecture; biological sequence adds high-fidelity reconstruction, regulation, transmission, diversification, and evolutionary accessibility to selected architectures. This framework connects inorganic catalysis, nanozyme chemistry, biomimetic systems, and biological catalysis through persistent physicochemical possibility coupled to increasingly powerful organizational control.

item.title: Light-induced signal enhancement in 13C solid-state NMR occurring in a flavin-tyrosine radical pair
item.description: “Light-oxygen-voltage” (LOV) domains are widespread flavin-containing proteins known for their numerous photosensory functions. Under illumination, some LOV domains form spin-correlated radical pairs (SCRPs), in which coherent spin evolution can lead to the buildup of transient nuclear hyperpolarization. In LOV domains, this solid-state photo-CIDNP (photochemically induced dynamic nuclear polarization) effect has so far been observed only with tryptophan as the electron donor. Here, we show that the effect can also be achieved with a tyrosine. The LOV domain of Methylobacterium (M.) radiotolerans (Mr4511-C71S) contains no tryptophan but five tyrosine residues. As it has been experimentally demonstrated, two of these five residual groups trigger an observable photo-CIDNP effect in the solid state. Theoretical simulations further suggest that the local proton environments could facilitate tyrosine oxidation through proton coupled electron transfer, thus favoring an observable solid-state photo-CIDNP effect.

item.title: Physical consistency and completeness in the data-driven modeling of microwave absorbing materials
item.description: Machine learning (ML) has been applied to the modeling of microwave absorbing materials, including the prediction of electromagnetic parameters and reflection loss (RL), yet the physical consistency of such models is rarely examined. This paper addresses two types of physical consistency problems in data-driven modeling: the physical inconsistency of predicted outputs and the physical incompleteness of input features. On the output side, we constructed a numerical integrator based on the Kramers-Kronig (KK) relation to test permittivity spectra output by ML models. The results show that none of the four examined spectra from three studies satisfied the KK relation, indicating that the model outputs markedly violate physical consistency. On the input side, we took a published MXene study as a case example. There is no thickness, which determines the RL jointly with other variables, in its feature space. Using physically consistent synthetic data, we conducted controlled experiments under two data settings and two partition schemes. It was found that without the thickness, the model captured only a limited part of the RL variance and could not distinguish the labels corresponding to different thicknesses. Adding the thickness restored the performance, with the R2 rising from 0.364 to 0.956 under the fullthickness setting. Finally, we further discussed three approaches to embedding the KK constraint into the modeling workflow. Our results suggest that physical consistency and completeness are necessary conditions for building reliable data-driven models, and that global integral constraints such as the KK relation cannot be learned implicitly from small samples.

item.title: Activity and selectivity descriptors for ethylene glycol electrooxidation from first-principle scaling relations
item.description: The electrooxidation of ethylene glycol emerged as a co-electrolysis anode reaction with the potential of valorizing PET-waste into industrially attractive chemicals such as glycolic acid. Although the focus on the reaction is increasing steadily in recent years, systematic means for catalyst developments are still lacking. Herein, we present a Sabatier volcano for ethylene glycole electrooxidation towards glycolic acid from a density functional theory-based limiting-potential analysis of late transition metal catalysts. A simple two-dimensional descriptor analysis rationalizes the enhanced activity of Pt and Pd compared to Au, as well as a reason for the latter’s near perfect selectivity towards glycolic acid. Furthermore, it provides target values for oxygen and carbon-affinity descriptors for ideal catalysts, where low oxygen affinity is beneficial to avoid surface oxidation at reaction conditions, while a high carbon affinity is beneficial for the initial activation and general smoothing of the free energy landscape of the reaction. Finally, we show that alloys are capable of linearly interpolating the single metals on the activity map, allowing the fine-tuning of the descriptors, if surface disalloying can be avoided.

item.title: Bayesian Optimization Outperforms Experts for Spectral Model Development
item.description: Indirect Hard Modeling (IHM) is a physically motivated approach for quantitative spectral analysis that can account for nonlinear spectral changes, provides loweffort calibration, and allows extrapolation. However, realizing the full potential of IHM requires careful adjustment of model parameters and spectral preprocessing settings, which is typically performed manually and relies on expert knowledge. To address this limitation, we investigate Bayesian Optimization (BO) as a strategy for efficient IHM parameter tuning with mixed continuous, discrete, and categorical parameter spaces. We couple six alternative BO frameworks differing in surrogate model and sampling strategy with Peaxact, a state-of-the-art commercial software for IHM. We compare the calibration performance and computation time. We develop four spectroscopic models based on literature datasets. The corresponding IHM models in the form of published parameter settings serve only as benchmarks and are not used to initialize the optimization. We thus demonstrate that IHM models can be automatically optimized without expert intervention nor prior selected configurations. The results show that BO outperforms the published models, ranging from marginal changes to reductions of approximately 50% in cumulative cross-validation RMSE and approximately 60% in cumulative prediction RMSE, 1 with mean runtimes of approximately five hours or less on a standard desktop computer, supporting practical applicability. Moreover, the configurations obtained via BO partially agree with the expert-selected settings, indicating that BO can identify reasonable calibration settings from scratch. Overall, the findings demonstrate that BO can improve IHM model accuracy, reduce manual calibration effort, and support the broader use of IHM in spectroscopy.

item.title: Linear-time Shape Alignment with ROSHAMBO3
item.description: Three-dimensional (shape) similarity is a useful primitive for virtual screening and molecular machine learning, but current open implementations are limited in performance by a quadratic inner loop across pairs of query-and databasemolecule atoms. ROSHAMBO3 achieves a 78–154× speedup over the previous open SOTA ROSHAMBO2 by using query-amortized Gaussian fields that make the inner loop linear combined with system-scale optimization at the algorithmic, GPU, and host layers, screening up to 55M query–conformer pairs/s on NVIDIA GPUs, with secondary CPU (x86, ARM) and Apple Metal backends. We further describe the human expert–AI interaction loop that guided the exploration and implementation of ROSHAMBO3 and discuss implications for the scientific software commons. ROSHAMBO3 is open source at https://github.com/kimiatx-oss/roshambo3.

item.title: CueMol3: combining a web-based GUI with a native engine for high-performance molecular visualization
item.description: Interactive visualization of large biomolecular structures and molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories is essential for interpreting simulations and structural models, yet existing molecular viewers force a trade-off. Viewers built entirely with web technologies offer flexible graphical user interface (GUI) development but are limited by JavaScript performance, whereas native desktop viewers cannot take advantage of the web GUI ecosystem. Here we present CueMol3, a molecular viewer that combines an Electron- and React-based GUI with a C++ computational engine embedded as a Node.js native addon. The engine writes geometry directly into reusable renderer buffers, which are passed to WebGL2 without copying on the JavaScript side. In benchmarks, CueMol3 updated the coordinates of 2.44 million atoms at nearly 60 frames per second (fps). For large MD trajectories (0.35–3.9 million atoms), it achieved frame rates up to about 15 times higher than those of the web-based viewer Mol* and outperformed the native viewer VMD. It also played back long trajectories that Mol* failed to load, with bounded memory usage. These results show that combining a web-based GUI with a native engine can match or exceed the performance of native applications. CueMol3 is freely available under the MIT License at https://github.com/CueMol/cuemol3.

item.title: Two-Step Recovery Kinetics with Distinct Time Scales in Stress-Softened Polyacrylamide-Carbon Nanotube Composite Hydrogels
item.description: Polyacrylamide-carbon nanotube (PAAm-CNT) composite hydrogels exhibit pronounced stress-softening alongside substantial CNT-induced toughening. Although stress-softening causes the reloading stress to drop significantly below the virgin loading stress, the underlying internal damage recovers given a sufficient resting period. We quantify the recovery dynamics using two independent metrics: the residual internal damage DR (defined as the hysteresis work loss) and the post-unloading residual strain εR. The recovery dynamics depend strongly on the applied maximum stretch (λmax): full recovery requires approximately 100 hours for λmax = 7, but takes less than 0.5 hour for λmax = 3. For λmax = 7, the recovery kinetics of DR and εR follow a biexponential decay characterized by two well-separated time constants: τfast ≈ 0.21 h and τslow ≈ 6.9 h. In situ small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) demonstrates that the strain-induced orientation anisotropy decays to the isotropic baseline within 0.1 h post-unloading. These results indicate that the fast mechanical recovery phase is governed by the rapid relaxation of CNT orientation and local Rouse-like relaxation modes of network strands, whereas the slow recovery phase, unique to large stretching, reflects long-range network rearrangement under topological constraints coupled with the gradual restoration of multipoint CNT-gelatin-PAAm physical interactions.

item.title: Ruthenium Catalyzed Reduction of N2O using MeOH as Hydrogen Source
item.description: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a significant contributor to climate change owing to its dual role as greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting molecule. Herein, the catalytic reduction of N2O to N2 using methanol (MeOH) as a terminal reductant was investigated employing a series of Ru complexes supported by proton-responsive picoline- and lutidine-derived pincer ligands incorporating N-heterocyclic carbene donors (CNC and CNN). Among the complexes examined, a Ru catalyst featuring a picoline-derived CNN ligand incorporating a secondary amine functionality displayed the highest activity, achieving turnover numbers (TONs) up to 417 after 72 h, in the reduction of N2O to N2. Under catalytic conditions, the formation of metal nanoparticles from this catalytic precursor was observed. These nanoparticles were independently synthesized and found to be catalytically active in the reduction of N2O with MeOH. Finally, control experiments further demonstrated that both homogeneous and nanoparticle species contribute to the overall catalytic process, participating in the methanol reforming and N2O reduction steps.

item.title: Zeolite ionic conduction genome
item.description: Zeolites combine diverse framework topologies, tunable compositions and exchangeable charge-compensating cations, offering a broad platform for solid-electrolyte discovery. However, how framework topology and composition jointly govern Li-ion transport remains poorly understood. Here we use machine-learning force fields to perform more than 40,000 molecular-dynamics simulations of nearly 2,900 zeolite topology–composition models spanning 263 zeolite framework types and a range of Si/Al ratios and establish a database of Nernst–Einstein ionic conductivity estimates for zeolites. We identify planar five- and six-membered rings as topological bottlenecks that impede Li-ion transport, linking local hopping barriers to long-range transport across diverse topologies. Within a given topological framework, the Si/Al ratio determines the Li content required for charge compensation and shapes the local electrostatic environment for Li-ion migration. In some frameworks, the competition between increasing Li-ion concentration and decreasing diffusivity leads to conductivity maxima at intermediate Si/Al ratios. Taking THO as an example, lowering the Si/Al ratio from 3 to 1 doubles the Li content per framework tetrahedral site but reduces ionic conductivity at 300 K by approximately 21%, showing that higher Li loading does not necessarily improve conductivity. Together, the database and mechanistic insights provide a foundation for co-optimizing topology and composition in zeolites for solid-electrolyte applications.

item.title: One Efflux Ratio, Two Validation Targets: Net Flux Asymmetry Is a Saturating Function of the P-Glycoprotein Pump Term
item.description: The bidirectional monolayer assay reports two apparent permeabilities. Their ratio, the efflux ratio (ER), is the endpoint against which computational models of Pglycoprotein efflux are scored. The same two numbers support two published readings of transporter activity: the net flux asymmetry as a fraction of the mean permeability, f = (ER − 1)/(ER + 1), and the pump term x = ER − 1. Which of the two a calculation should reproduce has not been examined. We show that f = x/(x + 2), a saturating map, so the two readings present different targets from identical data. For 1435 same-publication pairs with both members at ER ≥ 3 and mean permeability matched within twofold, the apparent difference RT ln(ratio) never exceeds 0.43 kcal mol−1 in the net-asymmetry reading. In the pump-term reading it is at or above 0.5 kcal mol−1 for 711 of the same pairs (49.5%) and reaches 3.41 kcal mol−1. The median ratio between the two differences is 5.6. Between publications, the efflux ratio of one compound differs by a median of 1.93-fold (62 compounds). A hydrogen-bond donor association persists when permeability is matched by measurement (48 of 63 publications, p = 3.8 × 10−5). A validation against efflux ratios can be interpreted only when the reading is stated.

item.title: Predicting the Fourth Analogue: Learning Stereochemical Transfer in Cyclic-Peptide Permeability
item.description: Combining stereochemical edits offers a direct way to explore cyclic-peptide chemical space. Once a reference peptide and two single-edit analogues have been measured, the modeling question is how molecular structure improves prediction beyond those three observations. We define this conditional permeability task using 1,154 chemically certified squares from four publications and evaluate transfer across 22 complete chemical families. The three measured analogues provide an accurate local anchor: adjacent averaging reduces source–family balanced mean absolute error from 0.319 for additive completion to 0.234 log-permeability units. Structural learning improves this informed prediction. A monomer-alignment difference kernel reaches 0.211 under family holdout, a 10% reduction, and kernelneighbor calibration reaches 0.217 under family holdout and 0.227 under source holdout. Supervision offers a second route to the gain: with the peptide representation fixed, changing raw-difference squared loss to hybrid pinball loss reduces source-held-out error from 0.285 to 0.232. Matched controls connect these improvements to the combination of structural representation, learning target and calibration by measured neighbors. Shared-edit and path-consistency diagnostics distinguish the information used by a correction, while the observed edit–background coverage identifies a concrete next experiment: crossing the same edits across new families under one assay protocol. The study establishes the predictive value of structural learning beyond three measured analogues and provides an independently usable task for testing that contribution. Scientific contribution. This work turns cyclic-peptide edit prediction into a fixed-information task in which local measurements anchor the target and learned structural relationships supply additional accuracy. Chemically certified queries, complete-family holdouts and matched learning comparisons identify how that additional information can be acquired and evaluated.

item.title: Intrinsically Safe Olefin Hydrogenation Catalysts
item.description: For exothermic reactions, such as olefin hydrogenation, the exponential rise in reaction rates with increasing temperature constitutes a safety hazard for large-scale reactions. Smart catalysts that switch themselves off when a reactor has become too hot could prevent accidents caused by thermal runaway. Here we report heterogeneous olefin hydrogenation catalysts that achieve turnover numbers exceeding 30,000 at 50 °C, but which reversibly switch themselves off at 120 °C. Their ensemble control mechanism for contra-Arrhenius switching allows them to operate efficiently in both gas and solution phase, and achieve a rate difference of ~700 between the ON and OFF states of the catalyst. Ensemble switching establishes a paradigm for the design of smart active sites that autonomously manage heat release in catalytic reactions.

item.title: Electrochemical Gas Bubble Production Drives Mass Transport Enhanced Destruction of Short Chain PFAS
item.description: Short chain perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) (C4 to C6), exemplified herein by the C4 molecule perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA), are considered harder to destroy than long chain PFAS. Herein, we report the use of an electrochemical flow cell containing two vertically orientated free-standing boron doped diamond (BDD) electrodes in a recirculating flow cell, treating solution volumes of 0.5 L. The cell is designed such 2 that recirculation flow zones (vortices) within the cell chamber are encouraged. This acts to increase the residency time for PFBA molecules and electrochemically produced intermediates in these flow regions. More importantly, with the cell orientated such that solution outlet is upwards, we show how bubbles produced at the electrode surface during water electrolysis further enhance the PFBA electro-oxidative destruction process. Increasing current density results in a concomitant increase in the density of gas bubbles leaving the electrode surfaces. This in turn locally induces microconvective enhancement of mass transport which is reflected in an increase in the firstorder rate constant for PFBA removal with increasing current density. At 700 mA cm-2 extremely high normalized volume/area first order rate constants for PFBA destruction are recorded (1 m hr-1 with a volume flow rate of 249 mL min-1). Coupled with the possibility of gas bubble-induced PFBA preconcentration and favorable hydroxyl radical production at the gas bubble-water-electrode interface, this leads to 100% defluorination efficiencies at current densities  175 mA cm-2 for ~ 20 mg L-1 PFBA in 0.5 M potassium sulfate.

item.title: From prototyping to daily practice: Chemically resistant 3D printed flow reactors for organic synthesis
item.description: The widespread adoption of flow chemistry in research remains limited by the cost and availability of suitable reactor equipment. 3D-printed (3DP) reactors could bridge this gap, but their adoption is limited because the thermal and chemical resistance of the printing materials are not yet fully understood. In this study, we establish an experimentally validated material selection platform that enables the selection and use of low-cost heat- and chemically resistant 3DP flow reactors in a wide range of synthetic applications. Reactors fabricated from polypropylene (PP), polyamide 6 (PA6), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and their composites by fused filament fabrication (FFF) remained leak-free at elevated temperature (>100 °C) and pressure (up to 20 bar). Glass- and carbon-fiber-reinforced materials enabled reliable operation up to 160 °C and 20 bar. The utility of the 3DP reactors was demonstrated in transformations relevant to the pharmaceutical industry, including alkylations, sulfonylation, Suzuki coupling, organometallic reactions, and photochemical processes. The resulting yields, productivities, and space-time yields were comparable to those obtained in commercial flow systems. These results should promote the broader use of accessible 3DP reactors and provide general guidelines for their safe and effective application.

item.title: H2O2-assisted vanadium catalysts on siliceous materials: support impact and V structure dynamics in CO2-promoted propane dehydrogenation
item.description: V-containing catalysts supported on purely siliceous materials are widely investigated for CO2-assisted propane dehydrogenation (CO2-PDH); however, the role of support properties in controlling the complex VOx speciation and its dynamic evolution under reaction conditions remains poorly understood. Here, we report a simple yet unconventional H2O2-assisted synthesis using V2O5 to prepare V catalysts supported on fumed silica, MCM-41, and Silicalite-1. Repeated H2O2 treatments progressively shifted V speciation toward lower-nuclearity VOx 2 species, with the extent of this restructuring strongly governed by the textural and structural properties of the support. V-Silicalite-1 catalysts achieved TOFs above 12 h-1, outperforming their counterparts by a factor of 2.0–2.6. Comprehensive characterization combining TPR, UV–vis DR, DSC, solid-state NMR, FT-IR spectroscopy, and in situ XAS revealed that high activity and stability arise from an optimal distribution of low-nuclearity and partially oligomerized VOx species, stabilized by the defective, hydroxyl-rich environment of Silicalite-1. Under in situ CO2-PDH conditions, these species undergo a highly reproducible redox cycle involving CO2 and propane, providing a dynamic V environment that sustains propylene productivity with time on stream.

item.title: Late Fluorescence Goes First: Dose-Resolved Suppression in Time-Gated Raman Spectroscopy of Recycled Poly(ethylene terephthalate)
item.description: The fluorescence of recycled poly(ethylene terephthalate) (rPET) was followed at two fixed spots with a time-gated Raman spectrometer (532 nm, 150 ps, 150 kHz), with the dose counted in laser pulses. At one spot, with the pile-up correction applied by the instrument software, the mean of the last three spectra, after 8.86 × 107 pulses, retained 0.208 ± 0.008 of the time-integrated fluorescence of the first run and 0.243 ± 0.009 of the gated fluorescence, and the Raman-to-fluorescence ratio increased by a factor of 5.52 ± 0.21 in the time-integrated data but by 4.87 ± 0.19 in the gated data. At a second spot, with a lower count rate, the fraction of the fluorescence inside the gate increased by a factor of 1.077 ± 0.011 with the correction and 1.043 ± 0.006 without it. Time-correlated single photon counting resolves the fluorescence decay within each acquisition: the late component is lost first. The Raman spectrum was preserved: all bands changed by a common factor. After pauses in illumination, the fluorescence was partly restored, by (2.4 ± 1.0)% per 100 s. This loss is consistent with the irreversible branch of the optical depletion proposed for solutions by Hamaguchi, Tahara, and Tasumi (Appl. Spectrosc. 1987. 41(8): 1265–1268).

item.title: Decoding Local Structural Changes in α-V2O5 Cathodes Associated with Mg-ion Batteries
item.description: Magnesium metal batteries promise higher energy density than lithium-ion systems, but their practical applicability is limited by the fact that cathode materials require elevated temperatures to achieve high reversible capacity at high potential. While the fundamental origin of this limitation remains unknown, the large potential hysteresis observed during cycling is a fingerprint of energyinefficient structural transformations that have never been resolved across both local and average length scales simultaneously. Layered α-V2O5 exemplifies this state of the art: it can deliver close to 300 mAhg-1 reversibly, but it requires a severe loss of crystallinity that obscures the structural rearrangements that underpin function. In this work, we use total scattering to reveal that, despite the severe loss of crystallinity, magnesiation of α-V2O5 remains a topotactic intercalation reaction 2 at the local scale. Structural interpretation reveals that the initial occupation of existing sites in the parent layered structure is followed by a shear and restacking of the layers to form a structure related to the δ polymorph of MgV2O5. The absence of structural coherency at the long-range is therefore a result of an accumulation of defects that prevent the propagation of the ordered stacking. Overall, our results highlight that, in many ways, intercalation of Mg2+ can follow the same structural rearrangements as Li+, but it induces a much higher level of defects that prevent long-range coherence and impose both energetic and kinetic penalties. This conclusion suggests that new rules of design are needed for oxides to become functional Mg battery cathodes. These rules must harness the evolution of defects and long-range order rather than just pursue simple bulk correspondence with Li-ion counterparts.

item.title: Closed-Loop Bayesian Optimization for the Synthesis of Amine-Grafted Resins for Direct Air Capture
item.description: Direct air capture (DAC) of CO2 requires adsorbents that combine high uptake with fast adsorption kinetics, yet whether these properties can be co-optimized remains unresolved. Here we couple automated high-throughput synthesis and characterization of amine-grafted porous polymers with multi-objective Bayesian optimization in a closed loop. Jointly optimizing equilibrium CO2 uptake and adsorption rate at 400 ppm CO2, we discover a kinetics-uptake trade-off described by a linear Pareto curve, uncovering adsorbents with order-of-magnitude higher adsorption kinetics than benchmark adsorbents at half the CO2 uptake. Three transferable synthesis-performance design rules are derived from the trained Gaussian process (GP) models and grafting with larger polyamines is established as a lever to extend the observed Pareto front. Process modeling shows that these adsorbents achieve twice the productivity of a realistic DAC process compared to the benchmark DAC adsorbent, Lewatit VP OC 1065. Beyond DAC, the framework provides a blueprint for other closed-loop multi-objective materials optimization studies.

item.title: On the role of boron in the direct dehydration of 1,3-butanediol into butadiene over Al,B-MFI catalysts
item.description: Direct dehydration of biomass-derived 1,3-butanediol (BDO) offers a potentially simple and bio-based route to produce 1,3-butadiene (BD). This is an acid-catalyzed dehydration reaction, which is usually carried out over either zeolites or metal oxides. While most of the studies are focused on initial activity, the relationship between nature of the active sites, stability and reaction mechanism remains poorly understood. In this study we show presence of the boron atoms in the zeolite framework along with aluminum enhances stability of the reaction. Intermediates conversion experiments identified 3-buten-1-ol (3B1OL) as a key problematic intermediate leading to C-C cracking products. IR spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations suggest that trigonal framework boron generates weakly Brønsted acidic silanol groups and that B sites provide additional covalent stabilization of the primary carbocation formed from 3B1OL, favoring dehydration over cracking. Al sites, in contrast, appear more efficient at converting BDO but provide less stabilization in 3B1OL conversion. We therefore propose that the complementary roles of these two sites facilitate the simultaneous improvement in BD selectivity and slower deactivation of MFI zeolites containing both Al and B atoms in the framework.

item.title: A mathematical model to predict Weissella viridescens inactivation by ultraviolet radiation
item.description: Lactic Acid Bacteria, including Weissella viridescens, are among the main spoilage microorganisms under modified atmosphere meat products, such as vacuum-packed products. Ultraviolet radiation treatment (UV-C) is a surface food conservation method able to reduce microbial load with minimal quality changes. Thus, the goal of this work was to obtain a mathematical model to predict W. viridescens inactivation under constant and variable UV-C radiation intensities. The Weibull model satisfactorily described the inactivation data. 2.35 seconds were necessary to reach 6 decimal reductions applying the highest UV-C intensity (1.93 W/m2) evaluated, and 12.4 s were necessary for the lowest intensity (0.56 Wm2). A dynamic model was stated to predict the behaviour of W. viridescens under radiation intensity variation. The proposed model was validated with experimental data and was able to predict the inactivation of the studied microorganism. The results of this work suggests that UV-C radiation is a hopeful treatment, due to a substantial impact on loads of W. viridescens. Thus, it was found that ultraviolet radiation is an efficient technique for the inactivation of W. viridescens, and that the obtained models form a suitable basis for the study of a possible application of this technique in food in which this is the main spoilage microorganism.

item.title: FlaN-a method for calculating morphologies of molecular crystals using a flat nucleus approach
item.description: We present FlaN, a Python program for predicting crystal morphologies from two-dimensional nucleation theory. FlaN constructs polygonal flat nuclei from step-edge energies calculated directly from intermolecular interactions and introduces an edge-density correction factor, K, to account for anisotropic molecular packing. Analysis of over 200 molecular crystal structures shows that inclusion of K reduces sensitivity to user-defined parameters and improves morphology predictions for systems where edge-site densities differ substantially between crystal faces. Calculated morphologies are in good agreement with experimentally observed habits for a range of single-component and multi-component crystals, including the three known polymorphs of 7-fluoroisatin and a number of other systems. FlaN provides a computationally efficient framework for exploring morphology and supersaturation-dependent shape evolution of molecular crystals.

item.title: Development Status, Not Potency: A Data Audit of the Public ADCNet Antibody–Drug Conjugate Evaluation Set
item.description: Background. Deep learning models for antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) activity are evaluated against several distinct prediction tasks: recognizing constructs assembled from familiar components, predicting unfamiliar combinations of known components, and extrapolating to unfamiliar antibodies or payloads — which a single reported accuracy does not separate. A second difficulty arises when the activity label itself combines experimental potency with clinical development status. ADCNet, a published framework integrating ESM-2 protein embeddings and FG-BERT small-molecule embeddings, reports 87.12% accuracy, balanced accuracy 0.8689 and AUC 0.9293 on its test set, and releases both its data and its code, making it a tractable case for examining both issues. Methods. We audited the released ADCNet evaluation workbook (50 constructs) and modelling workbook (435 constructs). Antibodies were identified by exact heavy- and light-chain sequence rather than by name; payloads and linkers by canonical SMILES. We cross-tabulated the supplied binary activity labels against development status, compared labels across the supplied activity thresholds, quantified overlap between training and evaluation components, examined the representation of drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR), and evaluated single-component reference predictors. Results. The 50-construct evaluation split is a subset of the 435-construct modelling file. Measured against the 385 held-in constructs, 33 of 50 evaluation constructs (66%) contain no component absent from training; 40 of 50 (80%) share a payload–linker pair with a training construct, and 10 of 50 (20%) share an exact antibody–payload–linker triple, differing only in DAR. Reference predictors fitted on the 385 training constructs and scored on the evaluation split reach 0.778 (antigen identity) and 0.773 (linker identity) against a 0.680 majority baseline, compared with the 0.8712 reported for the full model. Labels are near-invariant to the activity threshold: 415 of 435 constructs (95.4%) carry identical labels at all four supplied cutoffs spanning 1 nM to 1000 nM. Antibody names are not injective with respect to sequence: 154 names map to 149 heavy/light chain pairs, and one identical sequence pair appears under six names across 89 constructs, 20.5% of the corpus. DAR is interval-censored for 141 of 435 constructs (32.4%) and silently replaced by range midpoints. Within the evaluation split, where a development-status field is supplied, all 17 constructs with any clinical status are labelled positive without exception while investigative constructs are positive in 17 of 33 cases; the modelling file contains no status column, so this result cannot be extended corpus-wide. Conclusions. A single-component lookup requiring no learned representation reaches 0.778 on the evaluation split against a reported 0.8712, on a split two-thirds of which contains no component unseen in training. Labels are nearly invariant across three orders of magnitude of activity threshold, and identity harmonization by antibody name would place one sequence, under six aliases spanning a fifth of the corpus, on both sides of a held-out partition. These are properties of the released data rather than of any architecture, and each is verifiable from the public repository. We recommend grouping on sequence rather than name, reporting component-overlap and component-identity baselines alongside model metrics, reporting threshold sensitivity, recording censoring explicitly, and releasing the measurement-level data from which labels were derived.

item.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery from Code to Clinic
item.description: Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are revolutionizing drug discovery, transforming an inefficient system of trial and error into one based on predictive modeling and data analysis. This comprehensive review on the growing role of computational techniques and tools considers every stage of the traditional drug development pipeline. This paper discusses how novel frameworks, high-throughput data analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations advance the discovery process, from target identification and molecular screening to pharmacokinetic profiling and candidate prioritization for clinical trials. By analyzing a wide range of recent studies, this review demonstrates that these approaches significantly reduce the time required to generate new chemical entities. This paper focuses on the relation between curating data, designing models, and validating experimental results, which together determine the reproducibility and usability of computational outputs. Even though computational methods have yielded many successes, their application is limited by several challenges. Only when paired with high-quality experimental data and interdisciplinary expertise can these methods substantially reduce the time, cost, and uncertainty associated with drug discovery and development. Limitations, including poor data quality, inconsistent data reporting, and limited diversity in chemical and biological databases, continue to constrain accuracy. The lack of interpretability in the results of computational systems complicates regulatory evaluation and broader acceptance within the scientific community. Addressing these challenges involves data standardization, clear benchmarking, and integrating experimental feedback into models. All in all, the findings demonstrate that computational drug discovery is moving from its exploratory phase to a more important role in pharmaceutical research, and future discovery pipelines will increasingly depend on computational frameworks.

item.title: Substrate-Controlled Electrophilic Fluorination of Alkenyl Boronates: Direct versus 1,2-H-Migrative Fluorodeboronation
item.description: A general fluorodeboronation protocol that converts readily available alkenyl boronates into fluorinated alkenes under mild aqueous biphasic conditions is proposed. The method employs 1-chloromethyl-4-fluoro-1,4-diazoniabicyclo[2.2.2]octane bis-tetrafluoroborate (F-TEDA) as a fluorine source in the presence of KHF2, providing broad access to functionalized alkenyl fluorides from β-substituted and β,β-disubstituted alkenyl boronates, including cyclic, heterocyclic, aryl-, heteroaryl-, and alkyl-substituted derivatives, with good functional-group tolerance and preparative scalability. In contrast, αsubstituted alkenyl boronates displayed divergent reactivity, furnishing allylic fluorides through a rearrangement pathway. Mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations support initial electrophilic fluorination of the C=C bond followed by either BF3 elimination or 1,2-hydride shift, depending on the substitution pattern and stability of the resulting cationic intermediate.

item.title: Beyond the library ceiling: an accumulation-time rule for electron activated dissociation in data-dependent metabolomics, and the structural information it adds for conjugates, isomers and unknowns in human plasma and urine
item.description: Electron activated dissociation (EAD) reveals what collision-induced dissociation (CID) destroys or ignores: intact conjugates, radical backbone cleavages, and double-bond positions. In untargeted data-dependent acquisition, however, generic settings yield empty spectra, and the few EAD libraries available do not yet cover them. We quantified both limits on a ZenoTOF 8600 with a reversed-phase method in human plasma and urine. A 3 × 3 grid of accumulation time (35 to 210 ms) and candidates per cycle (5 to 20), replicated in a second plasma pool and in urine, shows that, at fixed electron energy, the accumulation time decides the outcome: 2.7% informative spectra with the generic 10 ms setting, 70 to 78% at 35 ms and 96 to 99% at 105 and 210 ms. The rule: the accumulation must cover the 30 ms electron reaction. At 105 ms and 10 candidates (1.4 s cycle), 4,200 precursors per injection receive an informative spectrum, 80% of whose fragments CID lacks. Against the public CID library, the plasma pools yielded 124 metabolites with CID but 55 with EAD, although 92% of the former carried an EAD spectrum: the ceiling is the library, not the acquisition. Beyond that ceiling, EAD read what the library could not. Of 36 urinary glucuronides of steroids, isoflavones, indoles, and bile acids, 32 kept the conjugate in EAD where CID gave the aglycone and the library named none correctly; methylxanthine, methylguanine, and dimethyluric acid isomers with identical CID spectra were separated; and 17 unannotated urinary ions received an identity or class, among them the glycation product MG-H1, named Bisphenol A by the library. Leucine and isoleucine remain unresolved at 12 eV, and EAD-cell background ions must be removed before interpreting low-mass ions. The duty-cycle rule, ion-count criteria, and annotated spectra are the starting material for EAD libraries of biofluid metabolites.

item.title: Cost-Bounded Evolving Guardrails for Chemistry Protocol Screening via Event-Pair Evidence Retrieval
item.description: Translating a published synthesis paragraph into a machine-actionable protocol is now routine, but judging whether the resulting steps are chemically safe on a given bench is not: frontier models recognise equipment at near-perfect accuracy yet fall to 0.28 accuracy on laboratory safety questions, and whole-text screening of a multi-step paragraph cannot point to which condition–effect pair justifies its verdict. We argue that risk lives at the level of event pairs, not paragraphs, and propose UHG, a cost-bounded evolving guardrail for screening heterogeneous chemistry protocols via event-pair evidence retrieval. UHG compiles text, tabular procedures, and figure captions into one event-pair space, retrieves condition–effect pairs as auditable evidence, distils a teacher’s evidence selection into a lightweight reranker, and evolves per-lab decision boundaries under a hard annotation and inference budget. On 50 catalyst-synthesis protocols with step-level risk labels, UHG reaches unsafe F1 of 0.72 at 0.13 of the cost of whole-text GPT-4o screening, outperforming Claude-3.5-Sonnet whole-text screening

item.title: In silico assessment of potential protein structural distortion by covalent labeling reagents
item.description: Understanding protein structure is fundamental for studying molecular mechanisms and diseases, as protein structure affects function. Covalent labeling (CL) of proteins is a method to gain structural insights of proteins that may not be amenable to other methods or where the scientific question involved does not require atomic detail. In CL experiments, solvent-accessible residues are chemically modified with specific or nonspecific labels. Proteins are then analyzed via mass spectrometry, where mass shifts corresponding to chemical modifications provide information about residue solvent accessibility and local chemical environments. The underlying assumption of covalent labeling experiments is that the presence of covalent labels does not affect the overall higher-order structure of proteins. However, comparatively little research has investigated whether exposure to free CL reagents, prior to covalent modification, can perturb protein structure. Here, we developed and validated force field parameters for eight commonly used CL reagents. We then performed molecular dynamics simulations of nine proteins exposed to these reagents at elevated temperatures of 425 K or 450 K to facilitate conformational sampling. Our simulations showed that exposure to these free labeling reagents did not induce substantial global structural destabilization relative to control conditions. In contrast, proteins exposed to 8 M urea exhibited an average increase in root mean square deviation (RMSD) of approximately 17 Å compared to the control and labeling reagent conditions. Overall, our results support the assumption that a protein’s structure is stable during CL experiments.

item.title: Redox Chemistry of the Cyclononatetraenyl Ligand: A Tale of Radical Coupling, Homo – and Möbius Aromaticity, and Comproportionation
ATLAS (Amine-catalyzed Thermal Linkage of Aggregate & Sulfur): Catalytic Valorization of Petroleum Sulfur Copolymer for Scalable, Photothermally Self-Healing Circular Pavements
item.description: Petroleum refining generates massive elemental sulfur surpluses alongside mounting municipal solid waste burdens.
