Although inverse vulcanization offers a viable synthetic route to convert surplus sulfur into thermoplastic binders, uncatalyzed reactions require elevated temperatures (≥ 159°𝐶), triggering toxic 𝐻2𝑆 and 𝑆𝑂2 off-gassing and severe matrix brittleness. Here, we introduce ATLAS (Amine-catalyzed Thermal Linkage of Aggregate & Sulfur), an eco-efficient paving composite synthesized via low-temperature catalytic inverse vulcanization. Employing triethanolamine (TEOA) as a nonvolatile nucleophilic catalyst depresses the activation barrier for 𝑆8 ring-opening (𝐸𝑎 < 68 kJ/mol), enabling complete copolymerization with waste cooking oil triglycerides at 80°𝐶 − 120°𝐶 within 30 minutes without hazardous vapor evolution. The crosslinked sulfur-lipid binder (ca. 22 wt%) is toughened with reclaimed crumb rubber and coconut coir micro-fibers, binding dense river sand and crushed waste glass aggregates (ca. 78 wt%). Integrated rice husk biochar imparts broadband solar absorption (> 92%), passively elevating composite surface temperatures to 35°𝐶 − 70°𝐶 under tropical sunlight to activate dynamic disulfide (𝑆 − 𝑆) metathesis for autonomous crack repair (>85% strength recovery). ATLAS satisfies heavy-traffic paving standards (SNI 03-0691 Class A and PN-EN 1338), exhibiting compressive strength exceeding 40 MPa (41.8 MPa), water absorption below 0.2% (0.16 wt%), and rapid 2-hour ambient demolding. Techno-economic analysis demonstrates an industrial factory-gate unit cost of IDR 3,254 (approx. $0.21) per 3.6 kg paver (IDR 125,230/m2, securing a 16.5%–30.4% cost saving vs commercial Mutu A precast concrete; IDR 1,200/unit under community zero-cost sourcing) alongside a 72.6% net reduction in cradle-to-gate embodied carbon (61.81 kg 𝐶𝑂2-eq/ton).

item.title: Antifungals silence a subpopulation of non-albicans Candida
item.description: Antifungal susceptibility tests report how much a drug slows a population, not how that slowdown is distributed among its cells. A culture can lose half its activity because every cell runs at half speed, or because half the cells stop while the rest continue almost unaffected. We distinguished these cases in Candida using a public dataset of 6,227 single-cell Raman spectra from seven strains of C. albicans, C. glabrata andC.krusei,grown inheavy water(D2O) and exposed toamphotericinB,voriconazole, micafungin or flucytosine. The deuterium signal, expressed as C–D/(C–D+C–H), separated metabolically active from inactive cells with almost no overlap, which made the shape of each single-cell distribution directlytestable.Wefittedgraded,all-or-noneandhybridmixturemodelsandestimatedthesilent fraction withbootstrap intervalsthatalsoresampled thereference populations.The twoC. albicans strains that were partially inhibited responded in a graded way in all seven conditions. In all three nonalbicans strains, 11 of 14 partially inhibiting conditions contained a silent subpopulation, with all four drugs;C. krusei reached 58% silent cells (95% CI 48–65%) under micafungin at 1 mg/L. At the same population-mean inhibition of about 40%, C. albicans had no silent cells while non-albicans cultures had 18–35%. Silent cells gave normal fingerprint and C–H signals, so they were intact cells rather than poor spectra. Bulk readouts cannot see this split; single-cell D2O Raman resolves it within six hours.

item.title: Raman spectra track neoplasia but not malignancy in mouse colon
item.description: Raman spectroscopy is often reported to stage colorectal neoplasia, but validation is usually done at the level of spectra rather than subjects. We reanalysed public spectra from a p53 deletion mouse model (47 mice; 485 spectra of normal mucosa, hyperplasia, adenoma and carcinoma) with leave-one-mouse-out validation, covariate tests and within-scan paired contrasts. Lesions were separated from normal mucosa with a balanced accuracy of 0.79 (95% CI 0.74–0.84). Adenoma and carcinoma were not separated (0.48), although spectrumlevel validation suggested 0.75. Within animals, a progression score ordered normal mucosa, hyperplasia and adenoma, and placed adenoma above adjacent normal tissue in all 20 paired mice, whereas carcinoma did not exceed adenoma. Genotype and sex left no trace in normal mucosa, but spectra drifted with acquisition order. In this model, Raman spectra track neoplastic change up to adenoma, while the apparent malignancy signal reflects animal identity.

item.title: Cooperative OH/CH-based recognition enables lithium chloride binding and extraction
item.description: Lithium chloride is the primary target of ion-pair receptor chemistry aimed at lithium recovery from brines and battery waste. Here, we report the ion-pair receptors for LiCl, built on a resorcinarene scaffold bearing lower-rim CH hydrogen-bond donors, which is crucial for stabilizing the anion in its binding site, combined with OH groups that serve a dual role as anion-binding hydrogen-bond donors as well as Li+ coordination sites. Six receptors were synthesized and structurally characterized by X-ray crystallography: monofunctional control 1, OH-bearing receptors 2-4, ester-functionalized 5, and ether-functionalized 6. NMR titrations in THF-d8 (1H, 7Li) show that receptors 3 and 4 bind LiCl as an ion pair with high avidity (K11K21 ≈ 108-109 M−2), overcoming both the strong competitive solvation of Li+ by THF and the aggregation of LiCl into clusters. DFT modeling of the 4⊃LiCl complex reveals a binding mode in which Cl− is held by aromatic and aliphatic CH groups along with two OH groups, while the Li+ is coordinated by two hydroxyl oxygen atoms and forms a contact ion pair with Cl−. Receptor 3 achieves solid–liquid extraction of LiCl (~34%) into chloroform, outperforming LiNO3 extraction despite the latter's lower lattice energy. Under liquid–liquid extraction (LLE) conditions, receptors 3 and 4 transfer Li+ from water into the green solvent 2-methyltetrahydrofuran (MeTHF), reaching up to 100% receptor saturation and maintaining LiCl extraction abilities in the presence of excess NaCl. These results establish CH/OH-based receptors as a new platform for lithium chloride recognition and extraction from aqueous to ethereal phase.

item.title: Generative molecular dynamics of Li-ion electrolytes conditioned on force-field energy and force
item.description: We generate all-atom molecular dynamics simulation structures of Li-ion battery electrolytes following from molecular centers of mass with a flow-matching model that reads the force field’s energy and its force at its own predicted structure. Molecular dynamics (MD) with a polarizable force field is the reference for electrolyte structure and transport, but each new formulation costs a full simulation. We train a two-stage generative model on around 45,000 NVT simulations of 69 species run with MU-PFF, an in-house polarizable force field. Stage 1 generates the molecules’ centres of mass (COMs) over time; Stage 2 rebuilds every atom from one frame’s COMs by flow matching on each molecule’s orientation, torsions and residual displacements. In the final Stage 2 model (EF), every network evaluation first predicts the clean structure, then computes the MU-PFF pair energy and its force there, and feeds both into the network’s first layer (physics self-conditioning). Read at the noisy intermediate state instead, the same forces were not used by the network (0.006 % of the loss). We validate with energies and with forces. The energy check scores generated against MD frames under the force field. The force check is the configurational temperature θ per degree of freedom, which is 1 for Boltzmann-distributed frames; we first confirm it on MD frames with induced dipoles (63 of 73 classes). Every decision rule was fixed before the run it decided. Against an otherwise identical control (SC), EF lowers the energy excess from +9.48 to +9.12 kJ/mol per molecule (paired difference −0.36, 95 % interval [−0.75, −0.27]; lower in 93 of 100 frames and in every energy term). A second training seed reproduces the gain (−0.48 [−0.70, −0.31]), with the seed-to-seed spread well below it, and on all 200 validation systems the difference is −0.53 [−0.66, −0.36]. EF lowers θ on raw frames in 40 of the 41 force-fieldconsistent rotation and torsion classes (median −16 %) and moves the carbonyl alignment toward Li+ closer to MD for every species. The gain is in molecular orientation, and it comes with the force: the same energy fed without its derivative (E) changes nothing measurable. It also holds on Stage 1’s generated centres of mass, at four of five Stage 1 step sizes and at every system size from 0.8× to 2.0×. Stage 1 itself, compared with MD on 23 systems, reproduces the density (within 0.3 % from composition alone), the Li+ shell and the positions of the COM g(r) peaks (median shift 0.00 nm over 740 species pairs), but its peaks are 12 % lower and its molecules diffuse 1.7–1.9 times faster than MD’s at its shortest step. Over 200 frames per system, every model reproduces MD’s Li+ solvation on MD’s own centres of mass, where the force’s effect on structure is mixed; on Stage 1’s, EF is closer to MD than E in 15 of 20 properties and further in none, within errors that are Stage 1’s. On 28 independently simulated systems containing 19 species unseen in training, the structure transfers. From the composition alone, Stage 1 gives MD’s density within 5 % in 23 of the 28 systems (median ×1.001) and the Li+ shell in the median (×0.98–1.00); on the systems’ MD centres of mass, Stage 2’s Li–O coordination is 4.5 % below MD’s and its torsion populations stay close (Jensen–Shannon divergence 0.025). The energy excess is +16.5 kJ/mol per molecule in the median (+3 to +70 across systems, below the in-distribution +9.1 in 8 of them); EF’s excess is lower than SC’s in 21 of the 28 systems, although the pooled test fixed in advance does not resolve the difference. Stage 1’s diffusion is 1.4 times MD’s in the median, but it pulls the least and most mobile systems toward the corpus’s range (×0.16 to ×13). Across Stage 1’s trained lags the Li+ shell and the COM g(r) do not depend on the step, but diffusion slows by 19–44 % and atom-level strain grows at long steps. Density, diffusion and the Li+ shell are intensive in system size; atom-level energies are not, and rise steeply beyond the largest training systems. These frames are not yet Boltzmann-distributed: in distribution, EF’s frames remain +9.1 kJ/mol per molecule above MD frames minimised the same way, and before minimisation their configurational temperature is θ ≈ 5 instead of 1. Closing this gap requires a Boltzmann finishing step, such as Metropolis-adjusted sampling under the full force field at fixed centres of mass, whose result θ can verify directly.

item.title: Equation Linking Rydberg Constant, Nuclear Properties, and Periodic Properties of All Atoms
item.description: The problem of the proton charge radius, its correlation with the Rydberg constant, and difficulties in determination of the Rydberg constant using hydrogen atom spectroscopy have been acknowledged. The correlation of proton mass radius with the Rydberg constant is not known. The goal of this study is to derive an all-encompassing equation that unifies the Rydberg constant, the mass radius of the proton, the atomic radii (otherwise called Bohr radii of atoms), and the average ionization energy. The enabling objectives of this study were to: fit the equation to the components of the composite constant (including the Rydberg constant and the mass radius of the proton) and other experimentally determined parameters, such as average ionization energy, to compute the Bohr radii of the first ten elements of the periodic table; verify the reproducibility potential of the equations by fitting the average ionization energy equation to the computed radii; and demonstrate that the mass radius of the proton (which is greater than the literature values of the proton charge radius) is the appropriate fundamental constant that bears a mathematical relationship with the Bohr radii of all elements. The methods were theoretical and computational. An inclusive equation was derived that correlates the Rydberg constant with the mass radius of the proton (~1.1017 fm) rather than the inconsistent, lower proton charge radius. Computational results showed that the ionization energies per mole (IE) in this study ranged between 99.99999944% and 100.0000051% of the literature values for elements with atomic numbers 3 to 12. Computations exploring a mass radius equal to 0.67 fm and a charge radius equal to 0.832 fm yielded values that ranged between 164.4302287% and 164.45%, and between 132.5731087% and 132.5892575%, respectively, of the literature values for IE. In conclusion, it is the mass radius of the proton that correlates with the Rydberg constant and the periodic properties of elements; if an independent experimental determination of the Bohr radius of any atom becomes possible in the future, the Rydberg constant can be accurately computed. A future study could expand this scope to include 10 additional atoms of higher atomic numbers. Keywords: Proton rest mass, Proton mass radius, Proton charge radius, Rydberg constant, Bohr radius of any atom, First ionization energy of some elements.

item.title: Conformation-Dependent Through-Space Interaction: Triplet-State Regulation for Dual Room-Temperature Phosphorescence
item.description: Dual room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) channels can arise from triplet states of different electronic character within a single molecular emitter, but controlling the contribution of each state remains challenging. Herein, we demonstrate that conformation-dependent intramolecular through-space interactions (TSI) can regulate triplet-state character and enable dual RTP channels from a single molecular emitter. Specifically, two benzo[g]indole (BI) donors are arranged at adjacent positions on a dicyanobenzene acceptor, allowing their intramolecular TSI to vary with molecular conformation. An extended BI–BI arrangement exhibits weak TSI and structured locally excited (3LE-like) phosphorescence, whereas a more closely facing arrangement exhibits stronger TSI and broad charge-transfer (3CT-like) phosphorescence. Electronic-structure calculations reveal that stronger BI–BI interactions enhance donor orbital mixing and favor BI-to-dicyanobenzene charge transfer in T1, rather than generating a separate BI–BI-centered emissive state. The relative contributions of the 3LE-like and 3CT-like phosphorescence channels vary with excitation wavelength, enabling distinguishable RTP outputs for multilevel optical information encoding.

item.title: Biomolecular Recognition Programs Fusion and Segregation of Orthogonal DNA Condensates
item.description: Controlling interactions between synthetic compartments is essential for building responsive, reconfigurable molecular systems. Here, we demonstrate that biomolecular recognition programs the fusion of orthogonal DNA-based condensates. To do that, we re-engineered ligand-functionalized DNA nanostars whose orthogonal sticky-end interactions drive phase separation into initially immiscible condensate populations. Addition of a bridging bivalent protein introduces heterotypic connections that promote condensate association, coalescence, and mixing. Through proteolytic cleavage of the biomolecular receptor, we can then restore segregation of the condensate populations. We demonstrate this approach using antigen-functionalized nanostars, with IgG antibodies inducing fusion and papain triggering segregation. We then extend the approach to thrombin-mediated fusion of condensates displaying aptamers for distinct thrombin exosites, followed by trypsintriggered segregation. A mean-field model coupled to phase-field dynamics reproduces the observed morphologies and suggests competition between antigen recognition and neighboring sticky-end bonding as a possible mechanism allowing efficient mixing. These results establish biomolecular recognition as a modular means of dynamically rewiring the composition and connectivity of synthetic compartments without redesigning the DNA interactions that drive their initial formation.

item.title: What should AI agents know? Explicit knowledge for trustworthy, sustainable materials research
item.description: Artificial intelligence can propose materials, interpret measurements and increasingly coordinate experiments. Yet reliable scientific autonomy requires more than capable models: research systems must preserve what is known, where evidence came from and which actions are justified. We argue that machine-actionable scientific knowledge is essential for trustworthy autonomous research, and that ontologygrounded knowledge graphs are a particularly powerful way of achieving it when scientific meaning must be shared across disciplines, systems and scales. Using The World Avatar (TWA) as a case study, we examine how ontologies, dynamic knowledge graphs and software agents connect models, literature, experiments and laboratory assets, and how ontology-derived tools can constrain large language model (LLM) actions. A reported design-to-synthesis study of a new metal–organic polyhedron demonstrates the integration of previously separate tasks, but not yet an environmental benefit or fully autonomous discovery. A material-passport example further shows how shared semantics can support industrial circularity assessment. We distinguish structural validation from scientific verification, and circularity indicators from demonstrated environmental benefits. The priority is not to create a universal platform but to build evidence-preserving research infrastructure whose scientific and sustainability benefits can be tested.

item.title: Organic Matter by Minimizing Electronic Noise Peaks and Low-abundance Peaks with Few Occurrences
item.description: 21 Peak reproducibility is a major factor that affects the reliability of Fourier transform 22 ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) spectra of dissolved organic 23 matter (DOM), which was addressed by a newly proposed workflow, namely parallel 24 samples representation by similar samples (PSRSS). The performance of the workflow was 25 validated by parallel measurements and experimental replicates. Inspection of isotopic and 26 homologous peaks in the PSRSS workflow enabled elimination of electronic noise peaks 27 and low-abundance peaks with few occurrences, significantly decreased the Bray-Curtis 28 dissimilarity, and improved the molecular formula assignment ratio with only minor effects 29 on the assigned formulae. The Bray-Curtis dissimilarity threshold (55% to 60% or quartile) 30 was proposed to cluster FT-ICR MS spectra for DOM samples with similar molecular 31 composition. The noise peak removal performance was further improved for the similar 32 molecular composition samples by excluding outlier spectra and less frequently occurring 33 peaks via the PSRSS workflow. Moreover, the reliability of DOM molecular 34 characterization was significantly improved by the PSRSS workflow. Overall, our findings 35 demonstrated the feasibility of the PSRSS workflow to serve as a reliable, labor-saving 36 method to remove electronic noise peaks and cluster spectra, yielding reliable spectral 37 information for multiple independent FT-ICR MS spectra. 38

item.title: Controlling Guest Selectivity in BINOL-based Pd2L4 Coordination Cages via Endohedral Cavity Functionalization
item.description: BINOL-based chiral Pd2L4 cages were successfully used as supramolecular hosts for the binding of sulfonate guests. Endohedral modification of the cages (OCH2OCH3 vs. OH) enables the modulation of the noncovalent host-guest interactions, which allowed for the chemoselective binding of anthraquinone-disulfonate regioisomers and the stereoselective binding of camphor sulfonate.

item.title: In Vitro Cascade Oxidization of D-Glucose to D-Glucaric Acid by Three Coenzyme-Free Oxidoreductases
item.description: D-Glucaric acid (GA) is one of the top 12 value-added biochemicals with broad applications in the detergent, polymer, pharmaceutical and food industries. The conversion of D-glucose to GA requires full oxidization for both C6 and C1 termini but these highly-selective oxidation of D-glucose remains challenging. Previous in vitro enzymatic pathways have obvious weakness, for example, up to eight enzymes used and the addition of costly coenzyme NAD. Here we develop an in vitro coenzyme-free minimal enzymatic pathway through six-electron oxidation catalyzed by three coenzyme-free oxidoreductases for the conversion of D-glucose to GA. This new-to-nature enzymatic pathway comprises an engineered galactose oxidase (GAO), glucose oxidase (GOX), and a newly discovered high-activity pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), together with catalase for hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) removal. Structure-guided engineering of GAO improved its catalytic activity on its non-natural product D-glucose by a factor of thousands relative to that of GAO variant A3.E7, achieving the complete oxidation of C6 terminus of D-glucose. Sequence-guided mining identified ALDH from Devosia limi (DelALDH), which showed approximately five-fold higher activity toward L-guluronic acid than the best reported ALDH. Three-step oxidization of D-glucose was implemented by stepwise enzyme addition of GAO, GOX and ALDH for its respective oxidation of C6, C1 and C6 terminus of D-glucose. This four-enzyme cocktail achieves a molar yield of 98.3% GA from D-glucose with a productivity of 0.89 ± 0.01 g L-1 h-1. This in vitro coenzyme-free minimal-enzyme pathway could open a better door to biomanufacturing GA from D-glucose instead of myo-inositol.

item.title: Process Analytical Technology Selection via Predictive Modeling and Human-informed Decision Criteria: Enabling At-line Quality Control in pMDI manufacturing
item.description: Industrial quality assessment often relies on time-consuming offline laboratory methods that delay operational response and limit timely process decisions. At-line process analytical technology (PAT) can reduce this delay by bringing measurements closer to manufacturing operations. Handheld spectroscopy is well suited to this purpose because it enables rapid, non-destructive measurements with minimal sample preparation. Its deployment, however, requires selecting both a device and a measurement protocol. Selection based primarily on predictive performance may overlook cost, measurement time, operator effort, and other implementation requirements. This study introduces a human-in-the-loop framework integrating predictive protocol optimization with stakeholderdefined multi-criteria analysis. Unlike existing approaches that treat predictive performance and operational requirements separately, the framework integrates both into configuration selection and subsequently validates the selected configuration under routine manufacturing conditions. The framework was demonstrated for predicting the color and viscosity of polymeric methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (pMDI). Six handheld spectroscopic devices were evaluated under controlled variations in lighting and container geometry as key factors in the protocol. SCiO combined with support vector regression (SVR) provided the strongest predictions for both properties. The analytic hierarchy process integrated model-derived performance with stakeholder assessments of cost, time, and operator effort. Following production-floor implementation, the selected configuration yielded R2 = 0.91 and RMSEP = 0.7 for color, and R2 = 0.87 and RMSEP = 39.46 cSt for viscosity. This framework provides a transferable approach for selecting and implementing PAT configurations that meet the technical and operational requirements for industrial adoption.

item.title: Crystalline Covalent Organic Frameworks Meet Low Temperature Hybrid Glasses: Synthetic Strategies and Interfacial Interactions
item.description: Hybrid glasses have attracted increasing attention due to their versatility and low melting temperatures, which make them promising matrices for composite formation. Covalent organic frameworks (COFs), in turn, offer high crystallinity, permanent porosity, and tunable chemistry, yet their poor processability limits practical applications. Herein, we combine both to develop COF@Glass composites that overcome this limitation. Two preparation strategies were studied in parallel using two different COFs, and the in situ melting of the glass in the presence of the COFs outperformed the alternative strategy and physical mixing, preserving the integrity of both phases while generating a distinct COF-Glass interface. This interface was investigated by X-ray pair distribution function analysis combined with principal component analysis, which provided insight into the chemical nature of the interactions between the components, and further examined by diffuse reflectance spectroscopy. This work establishes a route to COF@Glass composites, expanding the processing possibilities of COFs.

item.title: Parsing the steric and electronic contributions of a second-sphere tryptophan to IsdI-catalyzed heme oxygenation
item.description: Staphylococcus aureus IsdI is a heme oxygenase enzyme that degrades heme to staphylobilin products that are distinct from the biliverdin products of human heme oxygenase. IsdI contains an essential second-sphere tryptophan residue, and the relative steric and electronic contributions of this residue to IsdI-catalyzed heme oxygenation were unclear prior to this work. The W66Y and W66F substitutions similarly decrease the rate of IsdI-catalyzed heme degradation, but the reduction potentials of Tyr and Phe are significantly different. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) characterization of the wild-type (WT) IsdI reaction products indicates that a near equal mixture of staphylobilin and formyl-oxo-bilin is present in the crude reaction mixture, plus a smaller amount of biliverdin. Notably, WT IsdI exhibits a significant bias towards δ-staphylobilin production with this isomer representing 87 ± 1% of the staphylobilin reaction products. This is especially surprising considering that WT IsdI yields a near equal mixture of β- and δ-biliverdin minor products. The heme degradation product ratios, and their isomeric distributions, are different for W66Y and W66F IsdI. These data are consistent with a concerted rearrangement mechanism for the first oxygenation reaction catalyzed by IsdI, and the data for W66Y and W66F IsdI suggests that the reactivity of the meso-hydroxyheme intermediate depends upon the solvent accessibility of the active site. Finally, the regioselectivity of the third oxygenation reaction catalyzed by IsdI can be explained by a deformylation mechanism that includes outer-sphere electron transfer from the indole ring of the second-sphere tryptophan to the conjugated π system of the linear tetrapyrrole.

item.title: Clickable zinc fluorescence sensors for live cell imaging
item.description: Zinc fluorescence sensors are widely used to seek a better understanding of the role of so called mobile or labile zinc in the human body. In order to understand biological processes, click-chemistry is often used to immobilize a multitude of different molecules at precise targets. Here, we combine both techniques by incorporating a dibenzoazacyclooctyne (DBCO) residue into two zinc fluorescence sensors of the ZP-family. These new sensors, ZP1(5-Me2en-DBCO) (1) and ZP1(6-Me2en-DBCO) (2), undergo the bioorthogonal, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) with azides. We demonstrate the functionality of this click reaction in cuvette studies as well as in living HeLa cells. For the latter, we pre-treated the cells with tetraacetylated N-Azidoacetylmannosamine (Ac4ManNAz) to functionalize the outside of the cell membrane with azido-groups. Using this technique, both sensors could successfully be clicked onto the cell membrane. The sensors exhibited a robust fluorescence turn-on upon zinc binding in cuvette studies (7.7 (1) and 5.1 (2)) as well as a reduced turn-on in the cell studies (1.5 (1) and 1.9 (2)).

item.title: Microphase Separation and Water Accessibility in Crosslinked Polyurethanes
item.description: Polyurethane (PU) is one of the most widely used synthetic polymers, driving increasing interest in recycling strategies that promote a circular economy. Despite substantial progress in PU research, how atomic-scale organization governs its macroscopic properties and determines the accessibility of cleavable linkages to catalysts remains largely unresolved, limiting the rational design of efficient chemical and enzymatic recycling routes. Here, we address this gap with atomistic models of a heterogeneous crosslinked network formed from toluene diisocyanate and propoxylated glycerol. The models are built by combining Monte Carlo downsampling of chain length distributions fitted to experimental data with iterative crosslinking and molecular dynamics relaxation. They reproduce experimental densities to within 3%, indicate separate hard- and soft-segment glass transitions, and spontaneously microphase-separate through hard-segment aggregation. Within the hard domains, interchain NH· · ·O=C hydrogen bonds are the most abundant cohesive contacts, accompanied by aromatic ring packing. At the polymer-water interface, terminal amine and hydroxyl groups are accessible to large probes, whereas urethane linkages, like the urea groups of the hard segments, are buried within the network and reachable only by the smallest probes. Access to the scissile urethane bond is thus restricted by the network architecture, a constraint that recycling strategies for crosslinked PUs will need to address.

item.title: Ligand-Dictated Anisotropic Growth of Cesium Tin Bromide Nanowires at Low Ligand Concentrations
item.description: Cesium tin bromide (CsSnBr3) nanowires (NWs) offer promising optoelectronic properties as alternatives to Pb-based perovskites. However, their synthesis often follows lead-based protocols and overlooks differences in metal–ligand coordination. In this study, we employed the strong coordination between Sn2+ and an L-type amine ligand to develop a straightforward strategy for obtaining CsSnBr3 NWs. We reduced the ligand concentration by ~93% compared with their Pb-based counterparts. Notably, strong Sn–ligand coordination enables using low ligand concentrations, which further drives the equilibrium toward CsSnBr3 NW formation. By contrast, the same low ligand concentration insufficiently passivates Pb-based NWs, resulting in poor size control. Structural analysis reveals preferential crystal-growth orientation driven by selective passivation of Sn–Br-terminated facets. Time-dependent investigations show initial Cs4SnBr6 nanostructures progressively assembling into well-defined CsSnBr3 NWs while suppressing the competing phase. Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy reveals reduced thermally induced lattice softening and modified structural phase evolution in NWs compared with nanocrystals. Overall, these results highlight the need for developing tin-specific strategies rather than conventional lead-halide perovskite approaches, as demonstrated by our ligand-starved, amine-rich synthesis. These findings link ligand-directed anisotropic growth and phase retention to morphology-dependent lattice dynamics, supporting the controlled synthesis of low-dimensional tin-halide perovskites for sustainable optoelectronic technologies.

item.title: Machine Learning-Driven High-Throughput Discovery of Energetic Materials Based on Regioisomeric Pyrazole Scaffolds
item.description: The energy-safety trade-off remains the central challenge in energetic materials design. This study constructs a virtual library of 25,417 derivatives based on two regioisomeric pyrazole scaffolds and trains predictive models using Density Functional Theory (DFT) data from 413 molecules. Unlike conventional approaches, we systematically benchmarked three descriptor families and identified RDKit global physicochemical descriptors as superior to Morgan fingerprints, revealing that global molecular properties govern detonation performance in this regioisomeric system. Among six evaluated machine learning algorithms, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was identified as the optimal base model. Building on this, we developed a multi-task XGBoost framework that jointly trains four physically coupled properties, further improving average R2 from 0.891 to 0.927. Critically, SHAP analysis reveals that the amino group (fr_NH2) exerts a negative net contribution to detonation velocity—direct evidence of the energy-safety trade-off—and enables regioisomer-specific design rules. Screening the remaining 25,004 molecules and validating the top 20 candidates by blind DFT calculations yield mean relative errors of 3.02% for D and 5.76% for P, with the best candidate below 2%. This interpretable, multi-task screening paradigm offers a generalizable platform for accelerated energetic materials discovery.

item.title: Phase-Resolved Spectra of Charged Aqueous Solution Interfaces from High-Resolution Broadband Sum Frequency Generation Vibrational Spectroscopy (HR-BB-SFG-VS)
item.description: Phase-resolved sum frequency generation (SFG) spectra provide direct access to the complex nonlinear optical response of interfaces, which can be obtained either through direct phaseresolved measurement or by analyzing intensity spectrum. Recently, we demonstrated that phase-resolved SFG spectra of the neutral air/neat water interface can be obtained from highresolution broadband SFG intensity spectra using multi-peak Lorentzian function fitting (MLFF) with physical constrain with the knowledge of the absolute phase for the ‘free’ O-H peak. Here, we further extend this MLFF approach to charged air/aqueous interfaces of the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and the cationic surfactants cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB). Sub-1 cm-1 and high Signal-to-Noise ratio (SNR) high-resolution broadband SFG vibrational spectroscopy (HR-BB-SFG-VS) intensity spectra of the SDS and CTAB aqueous solution interfaces were acquired in the 2400-4400 cm-1 region and analyzed using a phase-inclusive multi-peak Lorentzian line-shape fitting. Since the C-H region spectra from the interfacial surfactant layer are with excellent spectral resolution and high SNR, they provided the internal phase reference to determine the phase of the whole spectra, including the O-H spectral features originated from the interfacial and bulk contributions of the water species. We demonstrate in this report that the whole phase-resolved spectra of the SDS and CTAB aqueous solution interfaces thus obtained are consistent with previously reported phase-sensitive SFG measurements. These results suggest that HR-BBSFG-VS intensity spectra with high-SNR can provide a practical and reliable route for obtaining phase-resolved spectra of the charged interfaces, forming reliable basis for future quantitative analysis and understanding of complex interfaces in general.

item.title: Sulfonated Poly(phenylene ethynylene) Redirects KLVFFAE Self-Assembly by Suppressing an α-Helix-like Intermediate
item.description: Peptides can assemble along different pathways, and the transient conformations they adopt along the way can influence the structure and properties of the final assemblies. How synthetic polymers alter these intermediate conformations and thereby control peptide assembly remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how poly(phenylene ethynylene) bearing sulfonate side chains (PPE) changes the assembly pathway of the amyloid-β fragment KLVFFAE (KE). Time-resolved circular dichroism (CD) measurements showed that 50 μM KE in phosphate buffer at pH 4.25 first displayed α-helix-like features and later developed a spectrum characteristic of βsheet structure. Adding PPE markedly reduced the accumulation of the α-helical intermediate and accelerated the progression toward β-sheet-rich fibrillar assemblies. KE fully switched to this alternative pathway near the critical aggregation concentration of PPE, approximately 5 μM. Stopped-flow fluorescence measurements showed that mixing PPE with rhodamine B-labeled KE produced a rapid fluorescence decrease followed by a slower decay. We propose a two-step model in which electrostatic interactions contribute to the rapid association of PPE and KE, after which the resulting complex may undergo slower structural rearrangement. These findings show that PPE can redirect the assembly pathway of KE and suggest a two-step interaction process involving rapid electrostatic association followed by slower structural rearrangement. This provides a strategy for designing supramolecular peptide materials by controlling their assembly pathways.

item.title: Synthesizing antikekulene with global antiaromaticity and high stability
item.description: Antiaromaticity is conventionally associated with intrinsic instability, posing a 22 fundamental challenge to the synthesis and isolation of globally antiaromatic hydrocarbons1,2. 23 Most known examples have been realized either in ionic states3,4 or through heteroatom 24 incorporation5-7 to relieve antiaromatic destabilization. Antikekulene (antiK), proposed by 25 Vollhardt in 19868, is an iconic globally antiaromatic hydrocarbon comprising alternating 26 benzene and cyclobutadiene rings whose inner and outer circuits both satisfy the 4n criterion. 27 Extensive solution-phase efforts toward its synthesis have failed presumably owing to 28 antiaromatic destabilization and/or severe skeletal strain9-12. Theoretical studies have also 29 debated whether antiaromaticity is the principal obstacle, and whether antiK can exist as a 30 stable species is unresolved13-15. Here we report surface-assisted synthesis of antiK on Ag(111) 31 via dechlorination and doubly [2+2] cyclization of σ-radical intermediates stabilized by the 32 surface and otherwise inaccessible in solution. Scanning probe methods and theoretical 33 calculations reveal chemical and electronic structures associated with global antiaromaticity. 34 Remarkably, antiK remains intact upon air exposure and can be extracted into solution for 35 mass-spectrometric validation. It shows negligible oxidation after one week in air, opening 36 avenues for future scalable synthesis. These results demonstrate that global antiaromaticity 37 does not necessarily preclude molecular stability and establish a surface route to globally 38 antiaromatic hydrocarbons.

item.title: Resonant doping design for ternary n-type oxides: the case of CdSnO3
item.description: Ilmenite CdSnO3 combines a dispersive, s-type conduction band with a ternary cation framework, which makes it a natural platform to test whether the doping rules established for binary transparent conducting oxides carry over to more complex hosts. Using hybrid density functional theory, we map the intrinsic and extrinsic defect chemistry of CdSnO3 for seven donors (F, Sb, Y, Ta, Nb, W and Mo) across its three sublattices, and combine it with first-principles electron transport. The donors fall into three classes: band-edge donors (F, Sb), decoupled resonant donors (Y, Ta, Nb), and self-trapping d donors (W, Mo), which release one surplus electron and trap the other. Niobium, which forms a localised polaron in SnO2, acts as a resonant donor in CdSnO3, which we link to the local geometry of the trigonal ilmenite site. The phonon-limited electron mobility reaches 584 cm2 V−1 s−1, and Sb grown under Sn-poor conditions gives the highest predicted conductivity, ∼1.7 × 103 S cm−1 at an electron concentration of 1.1 × 1020 cm−3, followed by Ta. Because the conduction band minimum is shared almost equally between Cd, Sn and O, orbital mixing with the dopant barely affects the effective mass, which reverses the Ta/Sb ordering found in SnO2. The remaining mass penalty is set instead by the distortion of the dopant octahedron. These results give transferable design rules for doping multication oxides.

item.title: Co-precipitation of Ag2O/Ag over Green Synthesized ZnFe2O4 for Photocatalytic Degradation of Organic Pollutants
item.description: Suppressing the charge carrier recombination in photocatalysis of wastewater based on ZnFe2O4 semiconductor can be achieved through the formation of synergetic effect between the p-n heterojunctions. In this study, Ag/Ag2O was co-precipitated onto green-synthesized ZnFe2O4. Ajuga Integrafolia plant extract was used as a capping and stabilizing agent in the green synthesis of ZnFe2O4. Thermal analysis, phase purity, chemical composition, microstructure, and elemental composition were investigated. The photocatalytic performance of the synthesized materials was evaluated by monitoring the degradation methylene blue (MB) under visible-light irradiation. The 15% Ag/Ag2O decorated ZnFe2O4 showed the highest performance efficiently 88.2% of MB within 80 min, compared with the green synthesized ZnFe2O4. Uncalcined 15% Ag2O-decorated ZnFe2O4, which showed efficiencies of 47.9% and 51.6%, respectively. The performance of the synthesized materials was also evaluated by varying calcination temperature and pH of the MB solution. The optimized composite showed best performance in basic media at pH 10. This study suggests that Ag/Ag2O/ZnFe2O4 nanocomposites have strong potential for organic dye and contaminant degradation.

item.title: A Free CAPE-OPEN Electrolyte NRTL Property Package for the CESAR-1 Solvent and a Transferable Equilibrium-Stage Column Methodology Tested on Four Pilot Plants
item.description: A free electrolyte NRTL model of the CESAR-1 solvent (aqueous AMP/piperazine) was implemented in the open-source framework Reaktoro with published parameters and made available as a CAPE-OPEN property package. It reproduces the experimental CO2 solubility in CESAR-1 with an average deviation of 25%, comparable to published models above 60 ◦C and higher at absorber temperatures, and forms the basis of a pilot plant comparison. A methodology is proposed for applying an equilibrium-stage column model across plants with different inlet CO2 concentrations, capture rates, configurations, packing heights and packing types, with load-dependent transfer units and three calibrated parameters, determined at plants with sheet-metal packings and held constant. In closed loop at the measured capture, the specific reboiler duty of four pilot plants, including a gauze-packed plant to which no parameter was fitted, is reproduced with average deviations of 1.4-8.2% (10.8% at Kaiserslautern including three runs with deep regeneration or inconsistent data), the optimum L/G is predicted with reasonable accuracy, and the effect of lean vapour compression is reproduced. The benefit of absorber inter-cooling is overestimated by a factor of 1.8-2.7.

item.title: Mechanochemical Degradation of Activated Carbon-Adsorbed PFAS and Fluorinated Gases
item.description: Fluorochemicals are widely used in modern society due to their unique and valuable properties. From the perspective of sustainable fluorine resource utilization, technologies that enable the recovery and reuse of fluorine from waste or captured fluorochemicals are crucial. However, efficient strategies for recovering fluorine from these materials remain limited. Herein, we report a mechanochemical strategy for the direct conversion of activated carbon-adsorbed PFAS and fluorinated gases into potassium fluoride (KF), a valuable fluorination reagent, by ball milling with potassium metal. The process proceeds rapidly and efficiently under solvent-free conditions. The method is applicable to a variety of PFAS, including perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA), and perfluorobutanesulfonic acid (PFBS), as well as fluorinated gases such as SF6, HFC-125, and HFC-23. This work provides a sustainable strategy toward a fluoro-circular economy through the recovery of fluorine as a valuable chemical resource.

item.title: Direct Observation of Cooperative Si–H Bond Cleavage by Tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane and Carbonyl Ligands on Tungsten(0) in the Catalytic Hydrosilylation of Imines
item.description: The catalytic hydrosilylation of unsaturated substrates continues to advance through the discovery of unique catalysts that reach hitherto inaccessible reactivity. Here, we report that W(0)-bound CO ligands mediate in cooperation with B(C6F5)3 the heterolytic cleavage of Si–H bonds, which furnishes a siloxycarbyne-like W–CO–Si+ adduct. This is commensurate with the activation of a Si–H bond by a Lewis pair comprising the metal-bound carbonyl oxygen and boron atoms. This reaction was used to develop a catalytic hydrosilylation of N-methyl benzaldimines that affords valuable N-methylbenzylamine derivatives; this transformation is sluggish with B(C6F5)3 alone but proceeds efficiently when the mechanism is shifted from a substrate-controlled to a catalyst-controlled one. This work thus repurposes metal-carbonyl complexes as distinctive Lewis bases, beyond their well-established role as precursors for metal-catalyzed transformations that proceed via bond-cleaving and -forming reactions at the metal center.

item.title: Water-Accelerated Hydride Transfer in the Oxoammonium-Catalyzed Oxidative Cleavage of Secondary Alkyl Methyl Ethers
item.description: The hydride-transfer oxidation of alkyl ethers by oxoammonium catalysts has hitherto been largely limited to primary substrates because secondary alkyl ethers exhibit intrinsically low reactivity toward hydride transfer. Here, we report that the addition of a small amount of water significantly accelerates the oxoammonium-catalyzed oxidative cleavage of secondary alkyl methyl ethers. The method accommodates both benzylic and unactivated aliphatic ethers, providing carbonyl compounds through selective C–O bond cleavage under mild conditions. This oxidation can also be accomplished in a siteselective fashion in substrates that bear multiple methyl ethers, including benzylic, allylic, and aliphatic methyl ethers; for example, two aliphatic secondary methyl ethers within a steroid scaffold can be differentiated. Furthermore, sequential in-situ reduction enables the one-pot conversion of methyl ethers into the corresponding alcohols. Our results of mechanistic investigations combining kinetic analyses, DFT calculations, and an independent-gradient-model-based-on-Hirshfeld-partition (IGMH) analysis support a model wherein water participates in a multicomponent hydride-transfer transition state stabilized through cooperative noncovalent interactions. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for water as an active participant, rather than a passive additive, in hydride-transfer catalysis.

item.title: False Confidence in Generative Samplers: Exact Physical References Expose Hidden Errors and Diagnostic Blindness
item.description: Learned samplers are increasingly proposed for equilibrium sampling and free energies in chemistry, and they are usually judged by self-normalized diagnostics such as the effective sample size (ESS). We show with an elementary proposition that these diagnostics are structurally invariant to the Boltzmann mass α of unvisited basins. Conditioned on not proposing a basin, the importance weights follow the law of the truncated system: the ESS stays high while the free energy shifts by −k_B T ln(1 − α) and the nominal delta-method interval contracts around the biased value, so coverage falls toward zero while the basin stays unvisited. In a toy double well where one basin holds 49.9% of the mass, a proposal putting mass 10⁻⁶ on that basin achieves a median ESS of 98% but covers the exact log Z in 0% of 400 runs. On exactly enumerated Sherrington-Kirkpatrick instances (n = 24), nominal 95% intervals from masked diffusion and a GFlowNet cover the truth in only 8% and 47% of runs at β = 2, while classical estimators and an autoregressive network (VAN-MADE) stay near 95%. A reverse check that scores the proposal on draws from an independent reference sampler flags the dropped basin where the forward Jensen gap is blind. A RealNVP flow trained by reverse KL on an analytic surrogate of the alanine dipeptide Ramachandran surface drops the C7ax basin (8.1% of the surrogate’s mass) and reports a median ESS of 79% with 10% coverage; the reverse check gives G_rev = 11.7 nats. Flows on model landscapes in up to 414 dimensions, including the real LJ38 potential, behave the same way, although one control with the correct support also miscovers, so a large reverse gap is not specific to a missing basin. Finally, all-atom simulations of chignolin and Trp-cage and a Langevin sweep of LJ38 size the effect and show its single-trajectory analogue: an unbiased run reports nothing about basins it has not reached. Omitting the Trp-cage native basin, 50.3% of our trajectory, would shift the free energy by 0.417 kcal/mol.

item.title: Local Chemistry of Na-Site Substitution in P2−NaxMn0.66Ni0.33O2 Cathodes for Na-ion Batteries. A First-Principles Study of Structural Fluctuations, Ion Mobility, and Charge Redistribution
item.description: Layered oxides emerge as promising materials as cathode in sodium ion batteries due to the possibility to avoid critical metals and the direct industrial transferability in lithium-ion battery factories. A key point is that the layered structure can host a wide range of cations, enabling the substitution as a strategy to improve key factors such as structural stability, electronic conductivity, ion mobility, etc. For that, it important to determine how the different substituents can affect these factors, to then mitigate side reactions and improve the desired mechanisms. In the present work, the effect of the interlayer substituent ions on the open circuit voltage, cation mobility, local structural fluctuations, and electronic structure has been investigated for P2 − NaxMn0.66Ni0.33O2 ( with x = 0.66 and 0.083) cathodes through Density Functional Theory. Calculated open-circuit voltages show that the dopants do not significantly alter the overall desodiation potential, while the local voltage response depends on the substituent identity and the sodium content. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations reveal that all dopants maintain the layered topology while inducing distinct local dynamical responses, with Mg and Zn producing the most rigid local environments and K the highest lattice flexibility. CI-NEB calculations and Arrhenius-based estimation of diffusion rates show that K facilitates the Na-ion hopping, and Ca maintains Na-ion migration barriers comparable to those of the pristine material, whereas Mg and Zn significantly increase the activation energy for Na inter site-hopping. Electronic structure analysis reveals a markedly different behavior between isovalent and aliovalent substitutions: at high Na content, divalent dopants locally promote Mn3+-like electronic configurations, while at low Na content the charge is primarily accommodated by the oxygen sublattice; in both regimes, divalent dopants enhance oxygen participation in charge compensation. These results provide atomistic insight into how Na-site chemistry governs the balance between ionic transport, electronic structure, and structural stability, offering practical guidelines for the local chemistry of high-performance layered sodium-ion cathodes.

item.title: Spectator Cations Regulate Li+ Solvation in Ionic Liquid Electrolytes
item.description: Organic cations are integral to the ionic network of ionic liquid electrolytes for lithium-ion batteries, yet their participation in lithium-ion solvation offers a design variable beyond salt concentration and anion chemistry. Here, we show that relocating the ether oxygen in the side chain of pyrrolidinium cations changes lithium-anion association and ion transport at a fixed lithium-salt mole fraction. Spectroscopy and theoretical calculations support reduced participation of N-ethoxymethyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium in the coordination network, termed a “spectator cation”. The ionic liquid electrolyte featuring a spectator cation exhibits a higher fraction of lithium-coordinated bis(fluorosulfonyl)amide anions, lower viscosity, and faster lithium-ion self-diffusion compared with electrolytes containing alkyl-substituted or alternative ether-functionalized cations. These changes accompany an increased anion-derived contribution to the solid electrolyte interphase and improved lithium plating/stripping efficiency. Related improvements in sodium electrolytes extend the cation comparison to a second alkali metal. The results identify the ether-oxygen position as a molecular design variable for adjusting local coordination and bulk transport together in solvent-free ionic liquid electrolytes.

item.title: Hives Under Attack- Pesticide Integration and Climate Change Effects on the Physiology and Genetics of Apis mellifera
item.description: Honey bee (Apis mellifera) survival and overall health are threatened by pesticide use and climate change. This review examines the damage these two threats inflict on honey bee population as well as how they interact, creating new, difficult problems to overcome. Pesticides such as imidacloprid and thiamethoxam integrate into bee hives at both the individual and colony level. In the nectar, honey, and wax, pesticides are present in every part of a hive. Pesticide integration damages larval development, immune system function, memory formation, thermoregulation, the honey bee genome, and honey bee lifespans, with these effects compounded across generations. The consequences of pesticide exposure are exacerbated by climate change, which changes flowering periods and bee bodies to become increasingly unfavorable to hive survival. Pesticide induced thermoregulatory dysfunction compounded with heatwaves and cold snaps can have devastating effects on the survival of a hive. Compounding evolutionary pressures from both pesticides and climate change, combined with reduced genetic diversity from dwindling bee populations put additional stress on the species. Future research involving hive wide longitudinal studies and radiolabeling of pesticides could help track pesticide distribution and identify the combined effects of pesticide exposure and climate change on a hive.

item.title: AGA Companion – A Searchable Reaction Database for Automated Glycan Assembly
item.description: Chemical synthesis of oligosaccharides is a critical tool to study the biological functions of glycans. To accelerate glycan synthesis, automated glycan assembly (AGA) was introduced 25 years ago. However, major chemical databases such as SciFinder and Reaxys do not accurately index these automated syntheses, leaving more than two decades of reaction data out of reach for both synthetic chemists and data-driven tools. Herein, we report the AGA Companion, a curated, comprehensive database with accompanying search tools that offers closeto-full coverage of all glycans and their glycosylation parameters produced through AGA. An analysis of the full dataset provides the first systematic overview of solid-phase glycan assembly, reveals hidden trends in glycosylation and aids future problem selection, thereby laying a foundation for new synthetic endeavours and a data-driven approach to automated glycan assembly.

item.title: Non-Enzymatic Electrochemical Detection of Acephate Using Graphene/Copper Tetraphenylporphyrin Nanocomposite: A Comprehensive Study with Multi-Technique Validation
item.description: The widespread application of organophosphate pesticides in modern agriculture has necessitated the development of rapid, robust, and cost‑effective detection methods for environmental monitoring and food safety assessment. In this study, we report a non‑enzymatic electrochemical sensor based on a reduced graphene oxide–copper tetraphenylporphyrin (RGO–CuTPP) nanocomposite for the detection of acephate, a representative organophosphate insecticide. Three graphene derivatives (graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, and pristine graphene) and tetraphenylporphyrin/copper tetraphenylporphyrin were synthesized and systematically compared as building blocks. Among all compositions, the RGO–CuTPP nanocomposite with a 1:0.5 mass ratio exhibited the most pronounced response toward acephate, with a linear range of 0.1–0.4 mM, a limit of detection of 0.054 mM, and a limit of quantification of 0.178 mM. The composite shows excellent reproducibility (RSD < 5%), operational stability, and high tolerance to common inorganic and organic interferents. Structural analyses confirm the successful integration of CuTPP on the RGO surface through π–π interactions and Cu–O/N coordination, which enhances electron transfer and provides specific interaction sites for acephate. Concentration‑dependent voltammetry supports a detection mechanism based on surface binding of acephate, leading to an increase in charge‑transfer resistance and a decrease in faradaic current. The sensor’s performance in spiked water and vegetable samples demonstrates its suitability for practical acephate monitoring, emphasizing simplicity of fabrication, good robustness, and compatibility with real matrices over ultra‑low detection limits.

item.title: Paving the Way Towards a Compact Complete Chiroptical Toolbox
item.description: Circularly polarised luminescence (CPL) spectroscopy is a technique with applications in materials chemistry, bioimaging, probing fundamental chirality, but conventional photo-elastic modulator CPL instruments remain bulky, expensive and slow. We report a compact single-channel CPL (SC-CPL) spectrometer that alternates left-and righthanded emission through a piezo-actuated pair of orthogonally aligned achromatic quarter-wave plates using a rapid CCD detector. This design minimises moving optics and eliminates the need for detector matching and pre-calibration. It can operate in various acquisition modes such as time gated acquisition mode for long-lived CPL emission and a quasi-continuous mode for short-lived CPL emission. Validation against a benchmark PEM-CPL system using a range of CPL emitters reproduced fine CPL resolution with high sensitivity, orders of magnitude faster. This blueprint SC-CPL reported herein paves the way towards the world's first complete compact chiroptical toolbox. This could lead to significant advancements with pivotal scientific and societal impact.

item.title: Multistate Potential Energy Surfaces from an Equivariant Core-Hamiltonian Correction to Semiempirical Configuration Interaction
item.description: Nonadiabatic dynamics needs several coupled potential energy surfaces at once. Fitting each state separately discards the electronic structure that couples them, whereas semiempirical configuration interaction in the style of the orthogonalization-corrected OMx methods obtains all states from one Hamiltonian and thereby keeps the topology of their intersections. We propose to build multistate surfaces by learning inside this Hamiltonian. An equivariant network predicts a geometry-dependent correction to the one-electron core Hamiltonian, the operator that already carries the orthogonalization corrections of OMx methods, while the two-electron integrals keep their NDDO form. Configuration interaction then yields all states, their gaps, and analytic forces from the corrected operator, and the whole model is trained end to end on reference state energies. For 1,3-cyclohexadiene with XMS-CASPT2 references, the correction lowers the three-state error of refitted ODM3 from 0.222 to 0.096 eV on held-out geometries and halves the error of every state and gap. Along a new nonadiabatic trajectory propagated on the corrected surfaces, it agrees with XMS-CASPT2 to 0.09 eV, compared with 0.46 eV for published ODM3.

item.title: Streamlining Lateral Flow Assay (LFA) Data Analysis: A MATLAB® Live Script for Integrated Batch Image Processing and Limit of Detection Determination
item.description: Manual quantitative lateral flow assay (LFA) analysis can span at least three software environments: image-analysis software such as ImageJ, spreadsheets such as Excel, and coding tools using MATLAB, Python or R. Repeatedly defining Test, Control and background regions of interest (ROIs) for individual strips, transferring measurements and performing separate statistical and calibration analyses makes data analysis for standard-curve experiments laborious and introduces opportunities for manual handling errors. We present a one-stop MATLAB Live Script framework for single-image and batch LFA image analysis and data analysis. For batch calibration, researchers supply a folder of cropped LFA images with concentration and replicate information encoded in filenames, select the analysis settings and click MATLAB’s Run button once. The automated workflow then extracts line signals, combines replicate measurements, generates the calibration curve and determines the limit of detection (LoD), without manual intermediate measurements or data transfers. The framework supports sandwich and competitive assays with colorimetric or fluorescent/chemiluminescent readouts for strips containing one Test and one Control line. Quantification uses baseline-corrected peak areas or peak prominences, with optional Test/Control normalization. Algorithm-defined measurement regions avoid the variability of manually redrawn ROIs, enabling reproducible image quantification when the same images and analysis settings are reanalyzed. Calibration options include four-parameter logistic, five-parameter logistic, Hill, Langmuir, linear and two-term exponential models, with two direction-aware, blank-based methods for LoD determination. Diagnostic visualizations, input validation and analysis checks help reduce signal-extraction and calculation errors and make remaining failures visible for easier rectification, while model coefficients and goodness-of-fit statistics support interpretation. By automating the intermediate steps within one analysis environment, this framework streamlines LFA quantification and reduces opportunities for errors arising from repeated manual measurements and data handling in laboratory research and assay development. This document provides a detailed user guide to use the two MATLAB Live Scripts – for single strip and batch analysis.

item.title: Surface Stability of Alloys and Intermetallics during Electrochemical CO Reduction
item.description: Alloy catalysts for electrochemical CO2 and CO reduction are often screened on idealized, bulk-truncated surfaces, yet adsorbates and the applied potential can change which surface is actually stable under reaction conditions. Here, we combine density functional theory with surface thermodynamics to test whether active sites identified from *CO and *H adsorption energies persist in atomically dispersed single-, dual-, and tri-atom alloys, substitutional alloys, and intermetallic compounds. Two-dimensional surface phase diagrams, spanning the electrode potential and the CO chemical potential, show that adsorbates can reshape both surface composition and termination. *CO keeps Pd at the surface of the Pd1Au single-atom alloy, while the stable termination of intermetallic compounds such as SnPd and GaNi depends strongly on the elemental chemical-potential reference. Depending on this reference, the *CO and *H adsorption energies shift by up to ∼1 eV, so a site that appears active on an idealized surface may not exist under reaction conditions. Adsorption-energy descriptors should therefore be evaluated on thermodynamically accessible surfaces, and predictions for intermetallic candidates are most robust when their predicted active surface is independent of the chemical-potential reference.

item.title: SmartReact: An Open-Source Python Package for Scalable Forward Synthesis Enumeration Built on Interpretable SMARTS Templates
item.description: Predicting which products can be made from a set of building blocks underpins library design, analogue generation, and synthesis-constrained generative modelling. Reaction templates encoded as SMARTS patterns are the standard tool for this forward synthesis enumeration task. However, existing approaches force a trade-off between chemical coverage, specificity, and the computational cost of applying large template sets at scale. We present SmartReact, an open-source Python library that resolves this trade-off through a template set built on SMARTS-RX, a hierarchical functional group ontology. SmartReact's templates are a combinatorial expansions over the functional group ontology of 406 patterns based on which functional groups interact in which reaction, so the library exposes only a few hundred distinct reactant-side patterns no matter how many templates it holds, and one classification per molecule resolves thousands of templates at once. Every prediction of SmartReact is traceable to a named reaction and an explicit set of functional group requirements, making results directly interpretable by chemists and straightforward to audit. New reaction types can be incorporated by specifying a SMARTS pattern and its functional group requirements, making the library easy to extend. A case study enumerating 536 001 unique products from 1 000 building blocks in 14.1 s demonstrates real-world utility at scale.Scientific Contribution: SmartReact contributes a large, expert-refined SMARTS reaction template library together with an open-source Python package designed to use it efficiently. The library's 9 770 templates spanning 37 medicinal chemistry reaction types are generated by combinatorial expansion over the SMARTS-RX functional group ontology, which gives them a chemical specificity and non-redundancy that auto-extracted libraries lack and, at the same time, a bounded reactant-side pattern space that makes them cheap to pre-filter.

item.title: Novel Class of Small Molecules that inhibits Yellow Fever Virus replication
item.description: Yellow fever virus (YFV) is a mosquito-borne virus that causes an acute viral hemorrhagic disease in humans. The high morbidity, recurring large-scale outbreaks, vaccine shortages, and the absence of approved antiviral drugs continue to make YFV a major global health concern. Therefore, the development of safe and effective antiviral agents against YFV remains an urgent priority. In this study, we used a para-menthane monoterpenoid diol and various aldehydes to synthesize a broad series of heterocyclic compounds with hexahydro-2H-chromene and hexahydro-2H-4,6-(epoxymethane)chromene moieties. Evaluation of the antiviral activity of the synthesized compounds identified compound 8k bearing a the hexahydro-2H-4,6-(epoxymethano)chromene core as a potent novel inhibitor of YFV replication in vitro. Compound 8k significantly reduced extracellular viral RNA copies and infectious viral load, highlighting its potential as a promising lead for the development of novel anti-YFV therapeutics.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Networks Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling end-to-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. For a feed-forward neural network (FNN) using extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs), embedding the EoS reduces the average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 8.67% to 5.57%. Replacing the FNN and ECFP representation with a graph neural network (GNN) using cyclic polymer graphs further reduces the average MAPE to 2.58%. Pre-training the models on PC-SAFT parameters for small molecules, followed by fine-tuning on polymer PVT data, yields additional improvements, reducing the average MAPE to 5.06% for the FNN and 2.15% for the GNN. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining an embedded EoS with geometric deep learning, and transfer learning for accurate polymer PVT predictions.

item.title: Structure Responsiveness of fluorinated PEGylated Au Nanoparticles in Physiological Serum.
item.description: Understanding nanoparticle (NP) - protein interactions is critical for controlling colloidal behaviour in biological environments. Here, we study how the introduction of fluorinated moieties into the PEGylated shell of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) influences interparticle assembly and interactions with protein. Combining microfluidic diffusional sizing (MDS) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), we revealed that exposing fluorinated hydrophobic groups does not compromise the stealth properties of PEG ligands. Remarkably, no lasting protein corona forms in biological media or fetal bovine serum (FBS), as evidenced by unchanged hydrodynamic sizes. Instead, SAXS revealed alterations in shell scattering length density, thickness, hydration, and interparticle interactions—effects that depend on the hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic ratio in the shell. These structural reorganizations suggest a transient protein layer with fast exchange kinetics that modifies interparticle forces without stable protein adsorption, offering crucial insights for designing advanced nanomedicines.

item.title: Organocatalytic hydroboration of allenes promoted by boron-based ionic liquid
item.description: The first protocol for the organocatalytic hydroboration of internal allenes affording Z-alkenylboronates is reported. Efficient and selective addition of HBpin to 1-aryl-3-methylallenes proceeds at room temperature and under solvent-free conditions in the presence of boron-based ionic liquid, 2-butyl-3-ethyl-3-methyl-1,3,2-oxazaborolidinium methanesulfonate, [BEMBox][OMs]. The reaction tolerates various functional groups on the aryl ring and exhibits high regio- and stereoselectivity. These features make the developed protocol a green alternative to the previously reported metal-based methods.

item.title: Tyrosinase-Like Monooxygenation Activity of Mono- and Dinuclear, Surface-Depositable Cu(I) Pyridinophane Complexes
item.description: Dome-shaped, surface-depositable organometallic complexes are a novel approach for the heterogenization of catalysts. In this context, we synthesized three copper complexes which are supported by different mono- and dinucleating pyridinophane ligands (thiacalixpyridine TCPy, dithiapyridinophane PyPS and thiacalixpyridazine TCPdz). Their monooxygenase activities towards monophenolic substrates were investigated and the influence of cavity size and nuclearity was assessed. While the mononuclear TCPy and PyPS complexes are almost inactive, the dinuclear TCPdz complex exhibits a high reactivity. Furthermore, monolayers of a TCPdz based dicopper(I) thiocyanate complex were deposited on Au(111) and investigated with the help of surface spectroscopy (IRRAS, XPS and NEXAFS) demonstrating the formation of a chemically intact monolayer.

item.title: How Effective is DFTB for Investigating Electrochemical Interfaces? A Study of Metal-Water Systems
item.description: Density-functional tight binding (DFTB) has recently emerged as a computationally efficient alternative to density functional theory (DFT) for modelling metal-water interfaces. However, electrochemical interfaces are inherently grand-canonical, and it remains unclear whether DFTB can reliably capture potential-dependent electronic response beyond equilibrium properties. Here, we systematically benchmark standard self-consistent-charge DFTB for Au(111) and many-body ChIMES-DFTB for Pt(111) against grand-canonical DFT. Using H2O, OH, and H adsorbates in vacuum and under explicit solvation, we compare two charge-control strategies available in DFTB+: an electronic-constraint counter-electrode approach and a fixed-total-charge scheme. Adsorption energies, Fermi-level response, charge partitioning, and interfacial forces are evaluated across charged interfaces. The electronic-constraint approach reproduces the potential-dependent variation of the Fermi level more faithfully than the fixed-charge scheme, whereas both approaches yield similar adsorption energies and charge partitioning on fixed geometries. We further show that adsorption energetics depend more strongly on the underlying Slater-Koster parameterization than on the addition of many-body ChIMES corrections. Explicit solvation remains the principal limitation, amplifying errors in electronic response and interfacial properties. These findings identify key priorities for developing transferable DFTB models for realistic grand-canonical electrochemical simulations.

item.title: Mooney Viscosity from Steady-Shear Measurements in a Rubber Process Analyzer
item.description: The Mooney viscosity ML(1+4) is still the most widely used flow parameter of unvulcanized rubbers, although it is a torque and not a viscosity. This work derives the relation between the Mooney torque and the steady-shear viscosity. An analytical solution for the rotor faces and the annular gap, corrected numerically for the corners, gives a conversion factor U(n), which depends only weakly on the flow index n. At a representative shear rate of about 1.2 s−1, the Mooney viscosity is, therefore, proportional to the viscosity. The relation was checked against steady-shear flow curves measured in a rubber process analyzer (RPA) on filled compounds, EPDM raw polymers and natural rubbers. On average, the measured Mooney viscosity is 1.23 times the calculated one, with a scatter of about 8 %. Thirteen industrial compounds from a second laboratory confirm this empirical factor without adjustment. With ML ≈ 0.90 η(1.2 s−1)/(kPa s), the Mooney viscosity is predicted within the reproducibility of the Mooney test. The cause of the factor remains open; elastic effects at the edge of the rotor are a possible explanation. A closed-cavity rheometer which is able to measure in steady rotation, and not only in oscillation, can thus provide the Mooney viscosity for quality control in addition to cure kinetics and flow curves, which are needed for the description of processes such as injection molding, compression molding and extrusion.

item.title: Flash Communication: PhI(OTf)2 Exists After All.
item.description: We report the observation of the parent PhI(OTf)2. This compound had been incorrectly invoked in many reports, but has never been observed before. Based on work on related systems decomposition pathways for PhI(OTf)2 arising from reaction with TMS-F to generate PhI followed by nucleophilic attack of PhI onto PhI(OTf)2 to generate iodonium cations were identified. This mode of decomposition is mitigated simply by working at lower concentrations, allowing for generation of relatively clean solutions of genuine PhI(OTf)2. It is shown however that this parent oxidant may not be useful as any oxidative process resulting in PhI generation will trigger decomposition by iodonium formation as a competing reaction.

item.title: Direct observation of valence tautomerism in sublimated molecular sub-monolayers
item.description: This study reports the first observation of a sub-monolayer molecular deposit prepared by sublimation on a conductive substrate of valence tautomerism (VT), an entropy-driven rearrangement of valence electrons between a metal ion and an organic ligand in redox-labile coordination compounds. To this end, a neutral cobalt(II) complex including two iminosemiquinonate redox-active ligands was thermally sublimated under UHV conditions onto highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG). Scanning tunnel microscopy and UV photoelectron spectroscopy, flanked by DFT calculations, were used to investigate the morphology and occurrence of tautomeric equilibria at the monolayer level. Temperature-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) experiments provided evidence of the intactness of the molecular deposit and reversible VT behavior, which is characterized by an incipient, reversible transition at T > 300 K. Finally, the quantitative estimation of the phenomenon was achieved using soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), which allowed the determination of the effect of surface deposition on the thermodynamics of the VT process. These findings establish the feasibility of preserving reversible valence tautomerism in surface-supported molecular layers and highlight the potential of VT compounds as active components in hybrid molecular spintronic architectures.

item.title: 60-Second NIR Regeneration of H-Phase Nb2O5 from Production Scrap: A Sustainable, Scalable Route to High-Capacity Anode Recovery
item.description: The escalating demand for high-performance lithium-ion batteries has intensified the need for sustainable electrode material recovery strategies that minimise energy consumption and processing time. Here, we report a rapid, energy-efficient nearinfrared (NIR) irradiation approach for the regeneration of niobium pentoxide (Nb2O5) from production scrap comprising a slurry of Nb2O5 active material, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder and carbon black conductive additive. NIR irradiation at 100% intensity achieves simultaneous and complete decomposition of both binder and carbon black within 60 seconds, as visually confirmed by a colour transition from dark grey to white, a result that conventional furnace sintering achieves only after 8 hours at 600 °C, representing a reduction of more than two orders of magnitude in processing time. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) confirms the disappearance of the crystallisation and melting transitions associated with the binder phase following both treatments. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) demonstrate that NIR irradiation preserves the crystal structure and morphology of the regenerated Nb2O5 to a degree comparable with conventional thermal treatment. Raman spectroscopy confirms the complete elimination of the carbon black D and G bands in the treated materials, validating conductive additive removal. Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) measurements show that the regenerated Nb2O5 anode delivers a specific capacity of 232.58 mA h g−1, comparable with the furnace-treated material and consistent with the high-capacity H-Nb2O5 polymorph. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) confirms redox peak positions consistent with H-phase Nb2O5, while kinetic analysis reveals a hybrid charge-storage mechanism dominated by solid-state diffusion with a minor capacitive contribution, underpinning the high capacity and electrochemical stability observed. These results establish NIR irradiation as a time- and energy-efficient platform for closed-loop Nb2O5 electrode regeneration, with strong prospects for industrial-scale battery recycling.

item.title: On-the-fly Neural Network based Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations of NH3-SCR over Cu-CHA
